utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes. I heard that you had something to raise, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Yes. I wanted to state the position of the Defence concerning the time we have available for this witness. This witness has more than 200 paragraphs. There are several hundreds allegations, very general statement which can and must be questioned, challenged, and refuted. If the Defence does not get this opportunity, then any of these allegations may become a basis for a sentencing judgement regardless of whether the Trial Chamber or an Appeals Chamber would give weight to this witness. I don't even have one full minute for each allegation which he expresses. And in addition to that, we still need to cover in full, Zvornik, Bijeljina, on the ground, Vojkan Djurkovic, Brcko, the supposed sins of the police of Republika Srpska and high officials of Republika Srpska and my and my family's connection with criminals and so on and so forth. The Defence can clarify and prove all of that if it is given the opportunity. If it is not, then it makes no point to defend oneself. With such witnesses who are so general and free to state unfounded claims, if the Defence has no chance to challenge that, and this is only a question of time. So I would ask to be given this day and tomorrow for this witness. It will be easier for the Trial Chamber to see everything, because these witnesses have managed to put the Prosecution on the wrong track, and they can do the same thing with the Trial Chamber, so as not to delude the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I notice that we were very efficient last week. As for Belgrade, this has not been recorded. We have the transcript of his testimony at the court in Belgrade. It was the trial of people from Zvornik connected with the Yellow Wasps, and the Trial Chamber should see this. The Defence will present that. We were efficient last week. You concluded that yourselves. Seven witnesses for five days, and for me personally and for the Defence as a whole, this rhythm was very exhausting, but if it is, we should have enough time available to question each witness as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me. Your microphone seems to be on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It appeared that one of the microphones was on. I just wanted to alert the Court, and I think the registrar took care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we allowed you seven hours for your cross-examination, and you have spent almost five hours, so two hours left. That's my understanding. If you use till the end of today, you will have in total nine and a half, extra two and a half in addition to the original seven hours. So that's the time you will have for your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will try to cover as many topics as I can in that time, but I'm afraid I might make errors due to speeding up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Dr. Karadzic, can I simply suggest that you concentrate on the specific matters and leave out the general ones. In terms of allocation of time, I think you'll be better served that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to raise a redaction of matter. It's about redaction of transcript, and I would like to do this orally so that the Defence also is aware of why we do that, but it needs to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go back -- go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're doing that, I would like to advise you that with respect to the Prosecution's motion for leave to reply concerning the ICMP motion, we object to grounds 1 and 2, and we don't object to them replying on ground 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Davidovic. I hope you had a good rest. Yes. We'll try hard to conclude your evidence today. In the meantime, I would appreciate it if you could concentrate on answering the questions in a brief manner. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I want to show you a document. Did you know the National Assembly of Republika Srpska adopted a law on the obligation to submit information about the commission of crimes and that I promulgated this law on the 4th of January, 1994, in early 1994. It obliged everyone who knew anything about crimes to submit the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D7835. 1D3785, excuse me. Unfortunately, the translation is not completed yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please have a look whether this is a decree on the promulgation of the law on obligatory submission of information about committed crimes against humanity and the international law.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please see the next page. As you know, the laws are adopted by the Assembly, and the president declares them to be in force.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says here that whoever has information or items which may be used to prove crimes against humanity and international law that were committed during internal armed conflict and the civil war in the territory of Republika Srpska and other territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, which began in 1992 and which as specific crimes are described under chapter 16 of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska is obliged to put these items or information at the disposal or, as necessary, submit them to a relevant body and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One can see from the law that it is emphasised what is the purpose of all this, but if you would allow me, I would make a comment. When I was in the territory of Republika Srpska in 1992, I informed and warned Minister Mico Stanisic that a team should be set up or a department or a separate organ which would be a part of the MUP and which would deal only with the crimes which had been committed and had not been investigated, though there was information about that. He agreed, but I can see that it was only in April 1994 that there was an attempt to do that. Was that too late? It's never too late, but perhaps this should have been done from the first day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you answered the question, and you proceeded to make further comments. I would appreciate it if you make your answers a bit simpler unless requested by the accused or by the Chamber. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify this, Mr. Davidovic. Do you agree that this is a law which obliges others who have such information and that perhaps the ministry or the government did set up specific bodies or the like, as you had proposed? Is there such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please see the last page, Article 6. It reads: "Whoever refuses to place at the disposal of a relevant body for the collection of information on crimes against humanity or international law which have been committed as described under Article 1, paragraph 1 of this law or who prevents such submission shall be sentenced for a crime by a fee or a prison sentence of up to one year." So do we have a punishment included here for the suppression of such documents or information?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the 65 ter number of this? It's 3750 instead of 7835. Yes. I confirmed it. That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI 1424, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3785 is actually 3785. That should be the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then there might be a translation as well. Fine. Could we now please have 1D3779.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is my order to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, to the Supreme Court-Martial, and the Military Prosecutor's Office dated the 15th of December, 1994 by which I order that there should be co-operation with the Supreme Court-Martial and prosecutor's office of the army in accordance with the law and that instructions be issued to security organs in order to enable the operation of judiciary tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just can't see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can see it in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. The 15th of December. Yes, I confirm that this order relates to your order on the activities the relevant organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is strictly confidential, that this is an internal document and that it says that the order must be executed by the 15th of January, 1995, and that I must be informed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1425, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see 1D3770.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please have a look at these two versions, Serbian or English, whichever you find more legible. On the 5th of January, 1995, the military prosecutor, Lieutenant-Colonel Nebojsa Supic, acted in accordance with my previous order and says: "In regard to the order of the president of the republic of 15th of December 1994, we enclose instructions," which I ordered should be drawn up and disseminated. Can we please see the following page? He had already drawn it up on the 29 of December, and on the 5th of January he sent it, and it is prescribed here what the military police and the security organs are obliged to do in order to help military courts and military prosecutor's offices. Do you agree that while you were there neither civilian nor military judiciary were fully developed and there were -- there was also confusion about the jurisdiction of the courts and prosecutors' offices?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please show the following page just for the witness's inspection. We don't have to read out anything, but I would like the witness to see what were all the things that were envisaged. It says here in the penultimate paragraph: "On the basis of collected information, security organs shall draw up a criminal report in which they will state the evidence which were found when information was being collected ..." And so on and so forth. Is this the usual ending of the previous procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Instructions are issued with all details about how to act. This is not contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to read through it or can you recognise this as the usual working procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is instructions on work. It is clear, and there is no room for any improvisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please see the last page. Would you agree that it is ordered here that it should be ensured that an on-site investigation is carried out, that warrant arrests should be implemented and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are all activities which are envisaged for criminal prosecution or as part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1426, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now please have 65 ter 13395.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, can we see from these documents that the time of chaos was over and that the rule of law is being implemented?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. This is already 1994 and 1995. After the Vance-Owen Plan, many things changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now ask you to have a look at this. It's Republika Srpska, the president of the republic is writing to the National Assembly of Republika Srpska. It is a proposal of conclusions in order to improve the situation in the domain of penal policy. Would you agree and are you aware that the president of the republic is authorised to send such proposals of conclusions to the Assembly, even proposal of laws and other documents?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. This is your right and your obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now please have a look at the overview. It says here in the first paragraph: "On the basis of information prepared by the Ministry of Justice and administration it shows that in 1994, out of a total of 175.527 cases the number of cases that remained undecided in the regular courts was 76.466 or 43 per cent. In other words, they did resolve almost 100.000 case.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or 49 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did not decide in 43 per cent; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in 1993, 49 were unsettled and then it says according to the data on penal policy in the regular courts in 1994, provided by the republican prosecutor's office, the situation without the Bijeljina senior public prosecutor's office is as follows and then we have the information. It's for 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The total is 102 -- 1.256 convictions. Of this, prison sentences 304 -- or 504? No, 304. And then fines and everything else. Can we please see the next page, and in English we can keep the one we see on the screen now. Now, after number 14: "Proceeding only from the number of convictions and approved appeals, I have concluded that on the whole the situation in the area of penal policies unsatisfactory." Can we see the next page in English and have the same page in Serbian. Which can have detrimental consequences, et cetera. Now it says: "Taking advantage of its constitutional powers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Karadzic please read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, without showing the proper page, the interpreters have difficulty in following you. Otherwise, please -- you have to slow down. We changed the page, and then you just kept that speed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian page is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was a preamble. Let us leave the conclusions, all courts, in English. Is it the case that I am suggesting to the National Assembly to adopt these conclusions: "1. All courts (regular and military) shall be required to step up their work on all cases, especially in criminal cases." And since we can all read for ourselves, do you agree that there are five conclusions here? We can't see the fifth in Serbian. The second conclusion is that all courts be required to pass more stringent sentences so that if sentencing range is 1 to 5, they should sentence to 5. Then the Ministry of the Interior should intensify its work on detecting perpetrators. Then 4, that the public prosecutor and supreme military prosecutor report to the Assembly every three months on the situation in the area of penal policy and the problems related. Can we see the last page in Serbian. "The working group for drafting of a uniform Criminal Code is required," et cetera, et cetera. You are familiar with our political system. Does the president of the republic have other tools at his disposal except to suggest to the government and the Assembly certain measures that he believes should be taken? Can he do anything else apart from the MUP, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, nothing except what can be seen from these orders. These are your constitutional responsibilities and powers, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1427, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, the Defence is required to shed light and elicit details concerning your statement to make sure what is what. In paragraph 158 of your statement, you described your encounter with Vojkan Djurkovic. He asked you, "Who do you think you are, protecting the Muslim?" Et cetera, et cetera. And then in his defence, he showed you a paper, a document, signed by Mr. Krajisnik authorising him to expel Muslims. In other words, to carry out a humane removal or transfer of the Muslim people using the police, et cetera. And then you say you approached Dragan Micic, an MP at the National Assembly of Republika Srpska. You told him what you had seen, that document, et cetera, et cetera, and Micic told you then that he was unhappy about the expulsions of Muslims and he had discussed the situation with Djurkovic himself. Djurkovic had shown him the same document. Djurkovic did not hide the fact that he had that document or who had got it from, and he said he had seen Krajisnik -- Micic had said he had seen Krajisnik about seven or ten days later, and Krajisnik told him to stay out of it. 65 ter, please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Karadzic repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7066.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a decision appointing a war commissioner's office for the municipality of Bijeljina, and the members are named. The first one is Dragan Micic, MP. Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't have English translation of this. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1428, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see from this that I appointed these people and authorised them to be war commissioners and to assist the authorities of Bijeljina; correct? These were very prominent people, including Dragan Andjelic, President of the Executive Board; Dr. Jovo Vojnovic, vice-president of the municipality; and a certain Mr. Arsenijevic, the manager of an enterprise; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now see 1D3673. Do you know that in the Krajisnik case, Mr. Dragoljub Micic, whom we call Dragan, made a statement? You mentioned it yesterday. He gave a statement to the Defence team of Momcilo Krajisnik. Do you recall saying that? Are you receiving me? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this statement by Micic. I'm just reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I mean in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We now ask Mr. Micic to give a statement for our case, and in that statement he says Vojkan did not show him any authorisation to expel Muslims, and he had no contact with Vojkan, in fact, and that he himself initiated with the police that Djurkovic should be arrested, which was done twice. And then it says the leadership of SDS Bijeljina filed a criminal complaint against Vojkan Djurkovic. All this is happening at the time when the SDS was the governing party in Bijeljina. Did you know that prominent people from the SDS and the municipal authorities filed criminal reports and Djurkovic was arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, I don't know that he was arrested. He was brought in a couple of times for certain incidents, personal settlement of accounts, something of that sort, but that he was ever brought in for ethnic cleansing or expulsions of Muslims, I didn't know. But if you allow me, can I say something about this statement by Micic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, but briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, he denies that I was ever with him, that he showed me that, and the distance between Vojkan Djurkovic and him is like 200 metres between their offices. And as he told me, as he says in the last paragraph, why did I state this. And after that conversation with me, he stopped any contact with him. That's not true. Instead, when I returned, he said to me, "Please don't mix me up in that. I don't want to get involved. I don't want any trouble." I am in touch with him to date, and we participated in a public debate together. We were sitting together, the three or four of us. So what it says in this statement, of course it's his right to say whatever he wants, but I have no reason to make up his involvement or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me read part of this, which is important for the record. "Based on the above, I assert --"

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I just wanted to correct you. What is denied by the witness has no bearing at all. You said it is important for the record. It is not. Unless this is to be admitted, reading out the content of the statement has nothing to do with any factual assessment. Take it into account.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just say that in this statement Micic said he would not say good day to you, but he said you were not in touch, and he says he holds it against you that you gave an inaccurate statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this statement be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I -- we don't need your assistance, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. There's no basis to admit this at all, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I wanted to read the gist of it. The gist is that this witness -- this gentleman, Mr. Micic, refutes what this witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Put the question to the witness. What is important here is the witness's answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In that case it has been answered. Can we now see 1D3672.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say you don't know that he had been reported by prominent representatives of the SDS for his treatment of Muslims. You know that he was brought in for other offences.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was brought in because he got into brawls with some people, but I never heard that he was brought in for ethnic cleansing of the Muslims. I've never had occasion to hear that, maybe you can show me something. I know that he did that during the war without running into any trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look. Is this a document from the president of the Bijeljina Municipal Assembly, chairman of the Executive Board of Bijeljina, president of the municipal SDS board, et cetera, to the public security centre?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Request to bring in and start proceedings against citizen Vojislav Djurkovic and his associate Risto Marjan from Bijeljina, because on the night of 22nd and 23rd July, 1995, without the knowledge or approval of the authorised representatives of Bijeljina municipality, they took away by force about 50 Muslims from Mount Majevica." And 2: "Likewise at about noon on 23rd July 1995 in a public place in the area outside the hospital in Bijeljina, before more than 100 people, Djurkovic publicly and loudly threatened and insulted the people's deputy, that is, MP Dragoljub Micic, saying that he would muddy the Drina River with a deputy." Does it mean he would throw the man into the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably what he meant. Let's just look at the date. That was written on 24 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say that he threatened he would take him to Tuzla himself and made other threats?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was not unusual for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see the next page in Serbian. Can you see the signatures of these people? We can see the signatures on the original report.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Dr. Novakovic is one of the signatories.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1429, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now look at paragraph 116 of your statement, 116. You say that Jelisic -- I'll read in English. [In English] "Jelisic asked me who I was and spoke for so long that the call was traced. So Jelisic was arrested only to be released by following day. Dr. Milan Novakovic, president of the Bijeljina Municipal Board of the SDS announced on radio that the Jelisic factory was the most productive at expulsion of the -- and murder of Muslims." [Interpretation] Is that the same Novakovic whose name we saw on the report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same Dr. Novakovic who stated in 1992 when those killings happened, camps were set up and Muslims were expelled from Brcko, he said that the most productive factory of this kind was the one that Jelisic ran, and that's what he said publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he proud of the fact or was he being sarcastic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think he had other motivations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How can you say he was proud of it? He was a psychiatrist, a very prominent person, and he was in favour, as we saw he advocated the rule of law and he was a member of the Assembly that was passing these laws.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I know Milan Novakovic very well. Before this war started, I took Milan Novakovic three times to a mental hospital for treatment for his alcohol abuse. I know him very well. I know his inclinations and weaknesses. I know that he had certain very bad times, because he was a chronic alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, see what you think about various people and how many people you find okay, but we'll just admit this document.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't comment. I only confirmed what I said in my statements earlier. I'm not talking casually about people. I'm only answering questions, and you asked me about that man.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D3775.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that this is my memo, dated the 31 of August, 1994, sent to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the MUP of Republika Srpska, and the command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, the president of the Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina, and the President of the Executive Board of the municipal -- municipality of Bijeljina, in which I informed them -- it reads, "I inform you that on the occasion of the latest" -- we have a problem with translation. "I inform you that on the occasion of the latest reports on the problems relating to the Muslim population in Bijeljina, in particular as regards the treatment of Muslims who are members of the Army of Republika Srpska, I have formed a working group with the following composition: General Bogdan Subotic, chief of the military office of the president of the republic; Goran Milinic, security advisor; Petko Budisa, assistant manager of the public security department of MUP. The task of this working group is to monitor the situation on the ground and submit to me a report with a proposal of measures. And you are obliged to present to me all available data and facts concerning this issue to the working group. Do you see that this commission was set up, that it consisted of highly-ranking officials and that it was instructed to see what the situation on the ground was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I don't know if you have the report of this commission. I would like to see it if you do, and I guess this has to do with the problems that the Muslims who were enlisted in the VRS were facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what the document reads.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here Muslim population, and in particular the Muslim soldiers in the VRS. Correct? The Muslim population. That's what it reads.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It reads so, but if you allow me, I think I can clarify because I think these were the problems which arose with people who were at the front, and meanwhile their families were rounded up and taken to the separation line and then allowed to go in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1430, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 65 ter 7953. I don't think we have the Serbian version of this one. This is my letter. It don't have to be broadcast if -- though I don't think there are any reasons not to broadcast it. Can Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff please tell us what her position is?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't see a problem with a letter being sent to the ICRC being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So as you can see, but let me not read it. Can you read English?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I will read it out to you, and then it will be translated. "[In English] This is a brief note to let you know that the recent events in Bijeljina and Janja involving members of the Muslim minority have been totally misinterpreted by the media as well as officials of international organisations such as ... [No interpretation]. "[In English] We are not, repeat, not conducting a policy of ethnic cleansing, nor are our local authorities in any way implicated in what has been going on. However, we recognise that the problem existed and it is my firm intention to solve it. A start has already been made: the regional police head has been replaced. I am also taking certain other steps to deal with this matter, but I ask you to be patient and let me get on with this. Finally, I ask you to remember similar events in -- in the Prijedor area some time ago. We had the same problem of extremists taking law in their own hands. We addressed that problem and solved it soon thereafter. The same will be true of Bijeljina and Janja." [Interpretation] Mr. Davidovic, the problems existed. You concluded yourself that the initial chaos began to ease as the rule of law set in. You saw that in August I sent a commission, and do you remember that at the time the chief of the police in Bijeljina was replaced, not because he persecuted anyone but because he was not able to prevent this? And you can see this letter in which Dr. Kuhn is informed about this. Do you realise that the existence of problems implies the efforts of the state and that the issue of the extremists is one that you cannot blame on the state policy and the state organs. The problem exists. It is -- this is realised, and then we work on resolving it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree with that. Can you just remind me, who was this chief of police that you replaced? I cannot remember. And then I will answer the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know when Vajo Andric was there. You know these people from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is why I asked you. I wanted to know who this was, who was replaced, and at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: September 1994.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been only Branko Stevic who was replaced at the time, because after September 1991, I don't know who else could have been there in that period. However, it doesn't really matter. Let me not enter into any arguments with you. It's obvious from this memo that you were aware of the facts, that there was pressure against you from international organisations and the public and that for this reason when you faced the problems you made efforts by writing the letter setting up commissions, removing the chief in order to change the situation. It's a fact and it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Davidovic, a part of your comment implies that I wouldn't have done it if there was no pressure. Did you see strictly confidential documents which were not intended for public use but, rather, addressed to organs of state in order to implement the rule of law?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. I said that earlier documents and this one which you presented show that there was a need and that you were making efforts but for what reasons? I suppose it was the public pressure. But one question from me then to counter this. How is possible that you personally promoted Vojkan Djurkovic and awarded him the rank of major and a medal at a ceremony at the square in Bijeljina in 1994? If you knew that Vojkan Djurkovic carried out ethnic cleansing throughout the war and that he only did that and that that was his only task, how is it then possible that it should happen that you would present him an award? Was it an award for the work he had done or for the acts he committed? Or what was the reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, do you stand by that, that this is correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this document admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You saw in this document that Prijedor is mentioned, and that I mentioned that we did something similar in Prijedor. Can we now please have D1138?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1431, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says D1138. It's already been admitted, but just to have a look, as I mentioned Prijedor, to see that these activities were carried out in Prijedor as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In which army did I promote this gentleman, and where did he receive this rank from me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Arkan's army. He was a soldier of Arkan's all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have any evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow down. The interpreter didn't hear your answer, Mr. Davidovic. To the question from Mr. Karadzic that -- whether you had any evidence of -- of the fact that he was in Arkan's army, he was a soldier in Arkan's all along.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question, if you allow, was whether the witness has any evidence that I promoted him, and I asked him in which army was he serving when I promoted him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vojkan Djurkovic was a soldier for Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. In the video-clip that we saw yesterday or the day before yesterday when there was a troop review in Bijeljina, at the head of the unit, when they were ready to line up, to his left or to our right was Vojkan Djurkovic. He was standing there at the head. He was a soldier for Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. All along, he was never engaged in the Army of Republika Srpska and he was honoured and awarded at the square, when the unit was lined up in front of the court building in Bijeljina. I think it was in 1994. Some citizens were present. This was a public ceremony; nothing contested about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In your previous answer that you said in your answer I quote: "How is it possible that you personally promoted Vojkan Djurkovic and awarded him the rank of major?" What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that in 1994, there was a line-up of this unit of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, in Bijeljina after some activities they had carried out in that area. Some of them were commended or promoted, and Vojkan Djurkovic was awarded the rank of major at the time and he was also awarded a medal. I don't remember which medal any more; I was not present, but I know that he was there, that there was this line-up, that there was a troop review and that this decision was publicly promoted and this honour was awarded to him personally by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he wasn't promoted by Mr. Karadzic, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that he promoted him personally, because who else could have promoted him to a higher rank, and who could have made this decision on his promotion, if not President Karadzic? He was the one who awarded honours and who initiated these extraordinary promotions and who gave such medals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I -- do I do that for every army or just the Army of Republika Srpska? Do I promote people in all armies in Europe or in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only have in mind the Army of Republika Srpska, because you were not the military commander or president of all Balkans or any other country. I'm talking only about the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but Vojkan was not a member of the Army of Republika Srpska, was he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was in Arkan's unit, but you awarded particularly Arkan's unit. You promoted it as a unit which did much in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For the sake of Trial Chamber, this was video-clip P2858. Mr. Davidovic, this line-up of the unit which was part of the MUP of Republika Srpska at the western Krajina front, did it take place on the 29th of October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when that took place. I think it was in 1994. I just know that from the first day, even before the war events in Bijeljina, Arkan was present in our territory. First of all, he organised a camp between Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a training camp to which members of the Serbian Democratic Party were sent, young people who were being trained and prepared for some events. I know that Arkan came at the invitation of the Crisis Staff. We could see this from documents. And I know that he waged war in Bijeljina. I also know that he went to work around Brcko and Zvornik just as he did in Bijeljina. He wanted to liberate these places, and I said that I saw his members at the Lukavica garrison in Sarajevo. This is all I said about this army. It was coming and going and passing through all along during the war. It was going to the territory of Krajina in Croatia, and I know that it could move freely through the territory of Republika Srpska. I also know that there were a number of conflicts with active-duty officers of the army between Arkan and his men and the forces that he was leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I will ask you to be very specific and to prove everything that you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us finish with this document first. What I said earlier about Prijedor, this was in April 1994, and in order to complete the investigation of the events and crimes in Prijedor, investigative measures and everything else. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that you wrote a memo and that it had to do with Prijedor. I also know that you said toward the end, I looked at the English version which mentions Bijeljina and Janja. I also know that the entire population of Janja was moved out and that 80, if not even 90 per cent of the Muslim population from Bijeljina were also moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you stand by that, by the claim that all the population of Janja was moved out and 80 to 90 per cent of the Muslim population from Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everyone from Janja, and at least 80 to 90 per cent of the Muslims from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll prove that easily.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have a look at the document 1D3791?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Davidovic, that Arkan between April 1992 and September 1995 was not present at the front lines of Bosnia-Herzegovina, rather, Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was present, but I know personally that in the month of June, when the corridor was opened - I cannot remember whether it was June or July - when he passed through Republika Srpska with his unit he was going towards Kninska Krajina when the corridor was opened. They were taking some aid there or something to them. That I know. After that, I don't know what happened, because then I left myself. I wasn't there all the time. I wasn't there on a daily basis in order to be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So he was travelling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Slow down, please. Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So he was travelling to Kninska Krajina and carrying aid, passing through Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he passed through Republika Srpska and Bijeljina. That is my view of the war, yes, when he passed through Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, can you see the transcript which is scrolling down a little bit in front of your -- on the monitor in front of you? Can I give you a tip? The timing you can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The timing you can start your answer is when the transcript stops, which reflects the interpretation of Mr. Karadzic's question is over. Thank you. Please bear that in mind. Please put a pause between the question and answer. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I do apologise. I will follow it in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that Arkan was on the front line in Serb Krajina, Croatia, and that he was taken prisoner by Croatia and that Croatia let him go without him standing trial at all?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, and I know that he was released. It is only now that some articles appeared in the newspapers saying how he was released, but this is more by way of comment, and I won't want to go into that. I know that he was arrested. I know that he was released without having stood trial at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that in the autumn of 1995, after the bombing of Republika Srpska, from the 28th of August until the 15th of September, Republika Srpska was attacked by the Croatian Muslim federation, which is twice as big, also Republika Srpska was attacked by Croatia, the Croatian Army, and NATO, along with all sorts of other factors that were involved.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. It was in all the media. Nothing was a secret. At that time, the Army of Republika Srpska sustained terrible losses, and everything that happened was organised, as far as I know, by the active-duty forces of the Republic of Croatia and the Muslim Croat forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina led by Dudakovic, and I also know that before that there was a conflict of this man from Bihac, yes, Abdic and Dudakovic. They had a conflict in the area of Bihac. But it is true there was an offensive. These people took part, supported by NATO forces, and allegedly they gave physical and logistical support to these forces and Arkan was directly involved in these war developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in that situation, volunteers were admitted only if they were among the ranks of the army or the police. Do you know of anyone who fought in the Krajina outside the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how people fought, but I know that I recently read this comment, made by General Manojlovic who was chief of General Staff and who was at the front line at that point in time. He said that he had problems with Arkan's forces in that area when these joint actions took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he have problems because Arkan was capturing deserters or were there some other problems? Remember that it was mentioned that he captured deserters?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. They said that Arkan found all of those trying to desert and then I assume he sent them back to their units. I read that recently. It just so happened I read it in a news magazine, Manojlo Milovanovic was talking about what he remembered, and he said that that was a problem that he faced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just another problem in relation to Krajina in the autumn of 1995. Did you hear of the extent to which civilian -- Serb civilians were suffering, Mrkonjic, elsewhere? Have you heard of the mass graves that were found there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that there were many mass graves and many killings, that the forces that were penetrating the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina were committing abominable crimes. I actually know of neighbours who were killed in that front -- on that front line, and they couldn't even find their mortal remains even after all the DNA analyses. They haven't even been buried properly. It is true that there was a great deal of retaliation and a great many persons were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we focus on this document that is here now. The Eastern Bosnian Corps is writing up a report on the session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska held on the 22nd of August, 1994, and it says in Pale, on the 18th of August, the 44th session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska was held at Pale, and it says what was done there. The subordinates are being informed about what happened, the tactical group of Majevica, but that means that other units were also made aware of this. So can we have the second page now. Maybe it's going to be the third page in English, so could we have that as well. I would like you to look at the fifth paragraph from the top of the page, "The Assembly decided ..." Until we find our way in the English version, please focus on this. "The Assembly decided that the new government should prepare a program of measures and tasks in the newly created conditions that would be discussed at the session of the Assembly on the 31st of August, 1994." Within an item on the agenda entitled questions and proposals by MPs, at the request of the MPs, at a closed session of this Assembly, the President of the Republic Radovan Karadzic, the Vice-President Nikola Koljevic, Speaker of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, and the representative of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, Major-General Zdravko Tolimir informed the MPs about the topic of political and security --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, impossible. Impossible to follow if you read it out in that speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. It says -- well, at the request of the MPs at a closed session, the President of the Republic, Radovan Karadzic, Vice-President Nikola Koljevic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Speaker of the Assembly, and the representative of the Main Staff and so on and so forth answered questions put by the deputies. Since it was a closed session, that is not contained in the transcript. However, let us see what General Simic's report was. Can we have the next page. The next page in Serbian, and we'll try to see where the English is. It's fine in Serbian and in English it's probably one page ahead. "The President of Republika Srpska condemned the engagement of the organs of authority of the Zavidovici municipality, in the expulsion of people from Vozuca, adding that the assessment that it was safer to live in Vozuca than in urban parts of Sarajevo where the front lines were on both sides of the street and where civilians were being killed every day, but they did not move out, and they withstood all Muslim offensives. The President of the Republic also condemned all cases of indiscipline, alcoholism, evasion of military service, criminal activities against members of the Army of Republika Srpska carried out by Vojkan Djurkovic and the group around him." What do you say to that? This is closed session of the session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska? What do you say to that? What do you say in relation to your assertion that I awarded and rewarded Vojkan Djurkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that you criticised him and said that he created some problems. However, I said that in spite of all of that, he was promoted and a decoration was conferred upon him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Give the OTP a document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to collect statements from persons involved, and I'm going to send them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Consciously, you are misinforming the OTP and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please put a pause. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have exhausted this topic. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted as Exhibit D1432.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you now please focus on paragraph 165 of your statement. This is what you say: "I recall having been told by Djurkovic that on one occasion when they expelled 100 to 150 Muslims he collected 150.000 to 200.000 marks. Djurkovic told me he was paid well for the authority to be in charge of the expulsion of Muslims from Bijeljina. Djurkovic talked publicly about giving money to Karadzic and Krajisnik. Djurkovic paid a certain percentage of money collected for each group of people expelled to Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik." Is that what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to see. So you're chatting with him, and he is taking you in his confidence and saying what kind of money he is collecting, and you did not file a criminal report with the police, no? Did you write up a criminal report after that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you allow me to wait for the typing to stop so that I could answer as instructed by the President of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not chatting with Vojkan. I did not have an opportunity to converse with him. I conducted semi-official or official talks with him. I had several contacts, very unpleasant ones, with him, and when I asked him once, "What are you doing? How can you be doing that kind of thing?" and so on, he said, "If I didn't have the right to do that, I wouldn't be doing it. And if I did not benefit from it like those who are telling me to do this." And I said, "Well, who is giving you the authority to do that?" "Well, I get paid for what I'm doing, and I'm paying further on, and it's easier to see --" I've already said that when he rounds up 300 or 400 men on a truck, he takes them to a special location and searches these people for two days. I said that even very old women were examined gynecologically because they were looking for money. And usually he would tell them, Take what you can with you, so they don't take too many things. People would take diplomas if they have any, and some clothes and their valuables. In these groups of 300 or 400 persons, there would be millions of marks and -- or, rather, about 500.000 marks. He publicly boasted about this. He didn't only tell me about it. He told everybody in town about all of these things that he bought during the war and that he took, and he said that he took part of that money collected to you and to Mr. Krajisnik and that that is why you gave him the right to do that and that no one, therefore, dared stop him. At the moment when he did that, the army and the police did not do anything about it, although they knew what was going on. They even received telephone calls from neighbours saying here they are, they're coming, but they didn't dare react. And then the problem was perpetuated. This is to say that this kept happening all the time, from 1992 more or less until the end of the war. That did happen. The international community knew about this, the international Red Cross. I don't know who amongst the authorities did not know about that and did not stop it nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us -- let us go back to this paragraph of yours. Was this chatting or was this an official talk?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot chat with persons like that. I can have an informal talk, but all of these conversations are aimed at providing information that I eventually wrote up and sent to my superiors. Several times I wrote about this to my superiors. I must say even to President Milosevic through Minister Bulatovic. I sent him a document asking him to try to prevent this kind of thing from happening in Bijeljina in any way he can. I don't know whether you have that kind of information here. I did inform my superiors about that, and the authorities in Bijeljina knew about all of this in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you talked to Vojkan Djurkovic, and there is an official report in this connection and a criminal report. If not a criminal report, at least an official note.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a criminal report but an official note sent to my superior, and I wrote up a memo on several pages about all of these things that were happening, and I asked Minister Bulatovic to send this memo further on to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you write this, that he admitted that he would gather 150 to 200.000 marks and that he gave a percentage to Krajisnik and Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where is this official note?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I had this official note. I don't have it any more. I don't know if it was found in the federal SUP or the documents that were before this Tribunal before. I don't know. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the time, Excellencies, so I don't think that I should call up a document now. Perhaps I can do it after the break, if you so decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, we'll take a break now. Before we break, I just have one matter. Mr. Tieger, the Chamber has considered your request of 29 June 2011 for leave to reply to the accused's response regarding further orders on DNA testing and ICMP. We will grant you leave to reply but only in relation to item 3 of the request, that is on the issue of whether further orders by the Chamber are still appropriate in light of the accused's response. Could this reply be filed by the end of the day today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As always, we'll try to do so, Your Honour. If it appears that the -- that that won't be possible, I will let the Court know quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, you seen your official note to Minister Pavle Bulatovic. You sent your note to President Milosevic. We know that President Milosevic is dead. Is Minister Bulatovic alive?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was killed in Belgrade. I can't remember the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you sent any official note to the MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I knew that they had all that information. They know because they are directly involved in all of these developments, and they know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were involved?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since when Vojkan Djurkovic was rounding people up in the streets the police was not intervening. Even when the citizens called them in they did not come. And at the station they would remain inside and only when the rounding up is over did the police come out into the street. They knew from the start that he was doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you are making inferences. If they are not preventing him, they are accessories. Make a pause, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am thinking quite naturally. If they see what's going on and doing nothing about it, that means they must have orders not to do anything. All the time Vojkan Djurkovic is talking about it publicly, and everyone knew the kind of person he was. He likes to boast. He always drops names, emphasises that he has contacts here and there. So they knew, too, who he was and that he was doing what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Help me make this clear. You are using analogy and making inferences, namely if somebody is aware that somebody else is doing something and doing nothing to prevent them, they mean -- that means they are involved and an accessory. You say that Vojkan Djurkovic is the kind of person drops names and brags about his contacts to show that he is untouchable.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you believed him, that it was not only bragging, that it was true.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say I believed him. I'm not saying that all he said was true. I'm only saying what I heard from Vojkan, and that's what I conveyed to you. How much truth there was in what he was saying, I don't know, and I wasn't asked about it. I'm only talking about my personal experience, what I saw and heard myself. Everything else is up to everyone's personal judgement. How much truth there was in Vojkan's words, I don't know. After all, I'm not the only one who knew about it. The state authorities had all this information beginning with the police and the secret police, state security and the army. Everyone was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can't speak on behalf of the OTP, but I believe the Office of the Prosecutor will kiss you when you bring that official note that you talk about.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's not appropriate to make such a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me just a moment. I presented to the OTP a written document stating that certain documents from Bosnia and Herzegovina had been taken away from me and that official note was among them. There is such a document, in any case. Now, what happened with the documentation that I submitted to my command, I'll be free to say that before I came to testify in the Krajisnik case, I asked to be given certain documentation. They were unable to give it to me. They said a lot of it was destroyed during the bombing because the federal SUP building was bombed, and they still haven't looked through the remaining documents to see what there is there. So they were unable to give it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Djurkovic tell you how he sent money to me and Mr. Krajisnik, by mail or personally?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, supposedly he took it directly, and he even said, "When I hand over a bag full of money, nobody will mind. And if I wasn't paying that money, they probably would have taken that right away from me a long time ago." He was talking about a nylon bag full of money. Whether that was bragging, whether it was a lie, I don't know, but he said it to me, and he said it publicly. Everyone knew about it more or less. I can't understand that you are now trying to say that you didn't know about it, that you didn't know about him saying these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Davidovic, we have all reports from the State Security Service. Nobody ever reported about that to me. At least we would have had those reports. Did you know that my office recorded every visit and every telephone call to me and that in these diaries and agendas there's no trace of any contact between Vojkan Djurkovic and me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you. I'm just telling you what I know. That's what I was able to hear and see myself. Now, why they didn't inform you, why your subordinates did not give this information to you, I don't know, but that was common knowledge. It was notorious. Everybody knew about it. That's why people kept quiet, and nobody dared do anything, because they thought it comes from the top, and they had to bow to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. You confirmed that you know you were sent to provide assistance to the MUP of Republika Srpska after a public appeal made by the Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, Milan Panic, and myself to provide help in clearing up and eliminating paramilitaries; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the same occasion the FRY prime minister, Milan Panic, and I made a public appeal to the Muslims to return to areas where there is no combat? I mean, those Muslims who had fled, they should return to areas where there is no more combat.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I believe such appeals were made, especially by Milan Panic who was rather free in his speech, and he often said things that ran counter to what was going on to -- in Serbia, especially contrary to what Milosevic and other people said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please stay on the question. Do you recall that we also made an appeal to people to return to areas where there is no combat?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. You may have said it, but I focused on what I was told, that he was summoned, told to go to Bosnia at the request of Prime Minister Panic and you to help the Republika Srpska in disarming paramilitaries. That's the only thing I had to focus on. It's possible that you also said that Muslims should return to areas they had fled earlier, but I don't think they could have returned, because everything was either destroyed or given to other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anyone respond to that appeal? Did any Muslims return to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say when I came to Bijeljina and restored peace to some extent, some people returned from Hungary, from Serbia. Some Muslims did return to Bijeljina. I knew some of them personally. I saw them at the border crossing in Bosnia, because we were just establishing a check-point on the border at that time, a police check-point, and I could see at that time that some Muslims were returning to their homes, believing that combat had stopped, especially in Bijeljina, that people were no longer being rounded up and taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I have to return to those people the money that I allegedly received from Vojkan? Do you have that information? Was the money given back to those people, and did I have to return my share as well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Many of them accused Vojkan of taking money from them. Nobody mentioned you, and the fact that Vojkan says that he paid off you and Krajisnik is a different matter. I haven't seen his statement. I don't know. I never heard that anybody was claiming money from you. Even the weapons that had been taken away are now being claimed back. I know that there are many problems with the Muslims returning to the area of Bijeljina and Janja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we briefly look at D473. Is this a summary from a working meeting of the leaders of the MUP, dated 20 August 1992, strictly confidential? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we look at English page 10, Serbian 7, or perhaps 8. Serbian 8, English 10. Look at the last paragraph. "In Bijeljina, the situation is relatively good, but it's much worse than it looks at first glance. The problem with the Muslim part of the population is increasingly complicated with the return of Muslim refugees and those who had earlier left and this was affected by the recent statements of Mr. Karadzic and Panic. Among this population there is a certain number of Muslim extremists, and it is estimated that a large number of citizens of this ethnicity have weapons." Do you see that even extremists felt encouraged to come back after my appeal and that of Mr. Panic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This confirms that some Muslims were trying to return, but they were unable to return to their homes and that created significant problems, but I don't know how Muslim extremists would have been treated at that time. When I was there in 1992, there were no Muslim extremists -- there were no extremists. People were so afraid. They were trying to be invisible. I even had a good friend, a Muslim. Whenever he saw me around town, he would look away, cross to the other side of the street to be invisible. When I stopped him and I said, "What are you doing, neighbour? Why are you so afraid?" He would say, "I'm not afraid for myself. You will have problems if you are seen with me."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, do you know about my very strict view against all type of crime and all sorts of criminals and especially corruption?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I must say I'm not aware of it. It's the first time I hear of it. And if you have any document about that, I'd like to see it very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we look at P4 briefly, an intercept dated 18 November 1991. P4. In addition to other criminal features of Vojkan's conduct and the conduct of other people, would you call it also war profiteering?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an intercept of my conversation with Predrag, late Predrag Radic, in fact, Vukic, Radic, and Brdjanin. One is the president --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mayor of Banja Luka. Brdjanin was an MP. Could we see page 3 in both versions. Can you see the fourth from above? Karadzic said, "So I asked him nicely, I said to him, Andjelko, don't you guys hang around with criminals. Please don't. Your career's at stake. And then he says, absolutely. And I say, he says you know, they're not criminals. If they're not criminals, he says only two or three are, then great. Two or three. Sit down with the military prosecutor and the two are three that are criminals can stay in detention, and the other ones can be released." And then a bit further down Karadzic says, "But there has to be an agreement, and it really has to be checked who is a criminal and who has to stay. We must not base our policies on criminals. Let Tudjman do that." And a bit further down there is a swear word, and I say, "I don't need Serbs like that. I don't need 32 tossers. They say that 20 of them were released right away." Do you can you see that I advocated that people for whom there are reasons to keep them in custody should not be released?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. I see that's what you're advocating, but while you were advocating such things, you were probably aware that at the time there was much crime in the area of Republika Srpska, much crime, much crime and much collusion between crime and people who were in high positions who were allowing this or they were sharing profits with someone, but objectively speaking, you must know yourself that crime was rife and widespread. And I see what you advocated but whether all this information was reaching you or not is something I couldn't know but I'm telling you what was really happening on the ground. I can see that you were -- your position was against that and you wanted people who were doing such things to be arrested. So I'm not contesting at any time the efforts that you were making in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please show the next page. Mr. Davidovic, did we call you to drink tea together or did we call you to help us about crime?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You called me to help prevent the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
