utterances.text: And something else. You gave me carte blanche. I have told the Prosecution that I did not have any prohibition, any restrictions or anything else. I was completely autonomous when planning activities and operations, arresting, bringing people in. No one ever told me don't do that or didn't allow me to carry out anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please have a look at the fifth or sixth line from above where it says not private businessmen here. "I don't have anything against the private businessmen," Karadzic says there, "but the war profiteering cannot be stamped out," and then there's a swear word. "These are war profiteers. They are not patriots." Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now please have a look at 65 ter 31672. 31672. This is my telephone conversation with -- rather, dated the 2nd of November, 1991, with Nenad Stevandic. He was a party man from Banja Luka. Can we please see the following page in both Serbian and English. And here down near the bottom, please have a look, Nenad Stevandic says: "Ah, he was here in Belgrade for two days and I don't know who he came to see. I believe that he mentioned you as well, and so ..." And Karadzic says, "He can't mention me. I will be in Belgrade. I will be in Belgrade as well and tell people to disregard it. Uzelac has carte blanche there. There is no way to have any paramilitary formation to embarrass us and do what they did." And then Stevandic says -- Can you see from this that others also referred to me, they mentioned my name, and that this is something that I'm denying here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It happened frequently, Mr. Karadzic, that people, especially if they had a criminal past or if they had such inclinations would refer to you saying with full conviction that they had your approval what they were doing. To what extent that could be checked at such time, I cannot say, but I heard very often that your name was mentioned in various situations, and I must say sometimes these were bad people, criminals, swindlers, and your name was mentioned in various kinds of situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a look. He says: @doctor, the problem is no the paramilitary formations. The problem is that they really did plunder ..." It's page 3 in Serbian in English we can keep page 2. "They really did plunder, and they really did share that with" -- and some names are listed, Mladjenovic, Savicic, and Andjelko. And then it goes on to say, Stevandic says: "They know that if these fall, the others will fall, too." And Karadzic says, "let them fall, they mustn't do that. We cannot rely anywhere." And Stevandic says, "God forbid." And then I say, "What we are doing, we must not build a rotten stone in the foundations of what we are building. We shall not rely on criminals." Is this also evidence that my position was that we had to build sound stones as part of the foundation of what we were building at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One can conclude that from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this intercept be admitted with all limitations as a MFI'd document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D1433, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 32054, please. 65 ter 32054.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is my telephone conversation with Mr. Stevandic on the 20th of December, 1991. Let us please look at page 2 in English and page 3 in Serbian. Stevandic says, on the previous page in Serbian, "I'm interested if that's a political game, that they be released, then we should say." And Karadzic says, "No, no." And then on page 3 in Serbian and page 2 in English: "Thieves are not national heroes and we cannot lie to the people" - this is what Karadzic says - "no, no, they are -- they cannot be released until the investigation is completed. If the investigation is completed, then they can be released or remain detained until the beginning of the trial." And then he wants to ask me if anyone ends up from Serbia if there are internal conflicts or showdown and then someone from Serbia could intervene. And Karadzic says, "No, no. Nobody from Serbia will intervene. No way. Nobody will stand up for criminals. Only when the investigation is over and there's no need for them to be in prison, then let them be released." And then a bit further down, it says, "There's justice. No discussion about that. You may tell that to Stojan. We stick to position of the rule of law and we will protect ..." Yes, in English we need the next page, please. "You may tell Stojan this, because we support rule of law and we'll protect both Stojan and Uzelac in that sense. There -- no one over there can behave against the rule of law." Would you agree there may have been problems for Uzelac as the corps commander and Zupljanin as the chief of police while they prosecuted criminals and that by this I'm saying that they have our support?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They could be exposed to criticism and have problems, and I can see from this that you are supporting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please have page 4 in Serbian and we can keep the page that we can see on the screen now in English. Karadzic says here, "yes, yes, yes. All that will -- there's no -- you may say to Stojan that I stand behind that. No one -- none of them are allowed to behave any differently from any decent citizen." And then later on he says that he will attack Brdjanin. And then I say, "If they attack Brdjanin and the others and commit a criminal offence, they will have to go to gaol again. So there are no problems, and politically I'll fuck them to pieces." Well, it's a swear word, no doubt about that. And then a bit further down: "A change of a political position and attitude regarding the legality of the state. There is none of that." Can we now please see page 5 in Serbian. Karadzic says, "we'll never rely on criminals, and they have to know that. We won't mix -- or get involved in the issue of their guilt. Let the court decide about that?" And a bit further down: "By making political movements, we will neither facilitate or make their position more difficult. Therefore, we are not going to make it easier or more difficult for them." And the following page in Serbian, please. "Therefore, that's out of the question. If they want to have an influence, the climate is somewhat different now and there's no doubt about them not being guilty. If the investigation is over, the judge had the right to release them, but the investigation must be over and then end either with a conviction or an acquittal. Therefore, such an attitude must be resolved." Would you agree that this means advocating the law and that this is not something addressed to the press? I'm telling that to my party colleague from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. There's no doubt about it. It's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this intercept admitted in the same manner as the previous ones?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D1434.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one more on this subject: 65 ter 0036 -- 30036.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is my conversation with someone from state administration. The previous one was a party official, and now I'm talking with Mr. Miodrag Simovic who is the vice-premier of the joint Bosnian government on the 8th of June, 1991, 20 years ago. Miodrag Simovic was not a member of the party, but at the proposal of SDS, he was the vice-premier in charge of the judiciary and administration. Perhaps you knew that. Can we now see page 2 in both Serbian and English. Seventh line from above Karadzic says, "Were you at the government session when he accused the parties leaders for interference?" Simovic replies, "No." And then a bit further down after Delimustafic, Karadzic says: "You can ask for it that Mr. Delimustafic writes down the names of the leaders who wanted to intervene. When did they call him and intervene. I never called him and I never ..." And a bit further down: "No, no. But that's why he shouldn't be allowed to get out of this now. He has to say whether it was Alija or somebody else, but then he has to say who to be specific when, which leader, and for which person. And then finally, why should he listen to anyone? If somebody committed a crime, why would he obey any party leader?" So the Minister of the Interior, Alija Delimustafic, said at the government session that some party leaders interfered with the work of the MUP and Radovan Karadzic requests the vice-premier, who is superior to Delimustafic because he is in charge of the judiciary and administration to clarify this and to make Delimustafic say out clearly who interfered with his work. So would you say that this is an intervention relating to these anonymous claims that someone was trying to interfere?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, this will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1435, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please focus your attention on paragraph 145 from your statement. You're talking about Zvornik and in the second sentence you say: "[In English] My opinion was that the RS leadership was more than happy to have a state of chaos continue in Brcko, Bijeljina, and Zvornik. The re-establishment of law and order would have made it difficult for the RS leadership through the SDS to continue war profiteering." [Interpretation] Can you now please look at this one, D456. Can we please show that one so that we can see what was being said at the Assembly of Republika Srpska. Let us have a look at this. These are the minutes from the 20th session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, and I would like us to have a look at page 59 in Serbian and page 55 in English. That was my speech before the Assembly. In English, 55, right, and Serbian, 59. It's the sixth line from the bottom of the page. "I'm saying that we've been given a lot of credit by the international community, that we are cooperative, that we want to work on humanitarian issues. That has assisted us a great deal. Do not worry about that. We do not need Manjaca. I wish all of the Green Berets were killed while they still had a rifle in their hands. However, if you took them prisoner then you have to observe the Geneva Convention. That has to happen. It also suits us to close this. Just not for them to appear on the battle-field." Can we have the next page, please. In the middle, the end of the first paragraph on this page and the beginning of the second one, I say: "There is an imminent threat of war. That is what we have declared. And if we need to declare a state of war for that to become an efficient government, then I probably say that we'll not be afraid to be firm when they exercise authority. It's -- power's not an easy thing, but you either have it or you don't. Some people say that is true. I am pleased when I see that in Bijeljina children are playing ..." And so on and so forth. Could I please have the next page. In Serbian it's 60 and in English it's 56. It says: "Please let us look at this and let us see what will give us sufficient authority to do our work relentlessly as of the next day, because we do not have the right to fool around with our people, not only with Republika Srpska but with the Serbian people and all Serbian lands. Further on it says the democratic party has to be tolerant, mild, and allow different opinions, but that cannot be the situation in state organs. That's why laws exist and that's why laws do not allow any ambiguity." And further down, it says: "The government, the ministers, commissioners, municipal authorities, the military police, they must all start functioning within three days or we're doomed. That's a must. Get rid of the shitheads, if they are not for the police. Return them to the front and bring to the front people whose hands are clean. Change the whole police force." Do you agree, Mr. Davidovic, that the president cannot do more than ask for these measures to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I think that that was right on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you whether you remember that Dragan Andan was a police inspector first and that then he was appointed acting chief of the CSB?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 65 ter 18400. Could we have that now, please. Now we're going to see why Dragan Andan was promoted. First of all, he was a police inspector. We're going to see that on the last page. Then he was promoted acting chief of the security services centre. Then he was suspended and we saw for what reasons. You yourself would have suspended him. Now, let's see why he was promoted. This is the 17th of June, 1992, just before you arrived -- or, rather, you may have been there already. It says report on supervision. Actually, this is 65 ter. There should be a translation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The fact that a certain document does bear a 65 ter number does not necessarily mean there should be a translation, but that should be confirmed by --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is your responsibility to offer the translation of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff is on duty today, I am not asking you to criticise her, but you may criticise Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to go through this carefully, because there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's another improper comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. That was by way of a joke. I could not resist, because you criticise us when we do not provide a translation. The OTP have this as a 65 ter document, and they did not provide a translation as well. I thought you should criticise them the way you criticise us, but I thought that Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff should not be criticised like a man would be criticised, but if that is inappropriate, then I withdraw what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's not waste more time. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will have to read out more than I would if we had a translation. It says: "Report on supervision and insight into the situation in SJB Brcko and SJB Zvornik and partly the situation in SJB Bijeljina." That is the public security station in Bijeljina. Could you please read this for yourself, and I will simply recount what this is about. Does this say that Danilo Vukovic and Dragomir Andan from the 29th of May until the 12th of June, 1992, carried out instructional supervision and provided indispensable professional assistance to the stations of Brcko and Zvornik and then it says that on the 29th of May, the basic functions of the Brcko station were not carried out, and it says there was no komandir of the police, the crime investigation service was headed by a national security official, but their work was carried out in a very superficial way. And then further down, it says: "With the assistance of the chief of the public security station, we managed to constitute the service as such." And it says that: "Along with proposals and suggestions from the public security station chief, we appointed top officials within the station itself." And then the last sentence says: "As for the functioning of the patrol service in the territory of the liberated parts of the town of Brcko, we establish this service thanks to the understanding of the military organs who allowed for 155 policemen to be withdrawn from the front line." Do you remember that during these first months of the war the police had to abandon their regular duties and go and defend the front line?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases. I knew about Brcko because Dragan told me about that when I got there. When we came to Brcko later, he told me about these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page. The middle of the second paragraph says: As we arrived, we looked into the lists of the reserve police force, also checked against the criminal records. After that, 21 persons who went through these records -- or, rather, who were cleared were sent to TO Brcko. Does that mean that they were sent to the military?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next page. Part of my answer was not included. Does that mean that they were excluded from the police and returned to the TO -- or, rather, the army?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of those who were cleared and who were found among the reserve police force were returned to the regular army, that is to say, to the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that for them that was a lot more unfavourable, to return to the TO and to the army and to go to the front line, that that was a lot more unfavourable than doing police work in town?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course. They all wanted to be on the reserve police force and to be policemen. It would be a lot easier for them, a lot better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In a way -- in this way the police was cleansed, and it was a kind of punishment, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that those who came in such a way had to leave, but it's obvious that persons who actually did have a criminal record and who were admitted without giving them clearance beforehand, this -- someone simply said, "As of today, you are policemen." This happened on a massive scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then it says: "The special unit of the police station of Brcko that has 24 members is working in an unorganised way at their own initiative, wilfully, and that is not allowed." Right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That kind of thing is not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph speaks about the crime investigation department. It says: "As we were in Brcko, this department was constituted and it started operating in keeping with the conditions there. The department started collecting intelligence and other information of interest to the crime investigation service, homicide, rape, murder, et cetera. Since most of them were admitted by the public security station of Brcko, it was agreed that intelligence should be gathered and that after that, as the armed conflict ended in Brcko, then in the territory of Brcko other measures should also be taken against the said persons." Could you now please look at the last paragraph: "The public security station in Brcko, as for paramilitary formations Captain Dragan, the so-called Chetnik units from the area of Bijeljina that are led by a certain Goran Jelisic and the self-styled Chetnik units from the area of Ugljevik. These units are actually exercising pressure against these public security stations and on two occasions -- actually, can we have the next page. An armed attack was attempted against the police station in Brcko. Did you know about that just before you arrived in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then further on it says that some goods were found, some stolen goods. The value of these goods was about 200.000 Deutschmark, and then it says: "Afraid of self-styled vojvodas, majors, generals, policemen still conduct their work with some fear. We have seen that these persons do not stop at using weapons even against their close associates." And further down it says somewhere that a certain Goran Jelisic committed crimes, rape, murder of innocent Muslim civilians. This same person was bragging about his misdeeds in Brcko and Bijeljina. Policemen are fearful whether he's going to draw a gun at them too if he says them and if a policeman looks at him in a way that he doesn't like, he would draw a gun at him? Had you heard of this fear and terror in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that. The first thing I did was try to arrest Jelisic as soon as I arrived in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on it says: "In order for the public security station to function in an unhindered way, we believe that all paramilitary formations should be expelled from this area. Also, from the territory of Serbia the arrival of paramilitaries should be banned altogether." And then a bit further down, it says: "We believe that it is indispensable to provide proper equipment to this SJB, especially communications equipment, teleprinters, telephones with neighbouring municipalities ..." and so on. Can we have the penultimate page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We do not see the text at all. We have no reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we saw that in the case of Brcko, there weren't even the right technical conditions for carrying out proper work.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was insufficient. These are very small hand-held radios that are given to policemen who are on the beat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what it says about the public security station in Bijeljina, somewhere around line 10 or 12 or somewhere after CSB Bijeljina: "We were present during such an armed rebellion, when 550 members of Chetnik formations led by Vojvoda Mirko wanted to use land, land, and other infantry and other artillery weapons to destroy the security building in Bijeljina." Can we have the last page, please. This was signed by Dragomir Andan and Danilo Vukovic. Did you know this Vukovic as well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did. He arrived when I came to Bijeljina, when I was sent by the MUP -- or, rather, he was appointed head of the general crime department, including homicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, after such proposed measures, the MUP promoted this man to chief of CSB, and he is also given to you as your liaison officer in your operation of doing away with the paramilitaries, disarming them, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was sent to Republika Srpska, I first went to Pale where I talked to Mico Stanisic and Cedo Kljajic. When a proposal was made for Andan to come from Brcko and to be a coordinator, Mico was against that energetically. However, Cedo Kljajic insisted, and also what it says here, that when he went to Brcko, he compiled a good report showing that he did have knowledge and professionalism. So that's what I was told when I came to Bijeljina, that Dragan Andan would be withdrawn from Brcko and that he would be appointed coordinator for me. After 10 or 15 days, Dragan Andan was appointed chief of the public security station in Bijeljina, acting chief, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of the centre of the security services or the public -- or the public security station?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre of security services for the entire region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From the level of police inspector to --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Head of the security services centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1436, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 1D3619. It need not be broadcast because there is a name that should not be broadcast for the person's own protection. It's not a guilty party, it's a witness. 1D3619.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this an order by the president of the Presidency, that is president of the municipality of Bijeljina, Cvijetin Simic, dated 8 April, 1992, prohibiting the sale of alcoholic beverages to uniformed persons in the area of Bijeljina and envisaging sanctions in case of violation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it look to you like fighting chaos or advocating chaos?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This looks like a decision to suppress chaos, but I can say with absolute certainty that nobody ever honoured that decision. It was only later in 1993 and 1994 that some catering establishments were closed down or fined because they violated certain rules or worked longer hours than allowed, but, yes, this is an order prohibiting the sale of alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see at the bottom that a person is appointed to a certain position, but that's a different topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1437 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see 1D3620. We're now on the subject of Bijeljina, and while we're on it, let's see what the authorities in Bijeljina were trying to do. 1D3620. 8 April 1992, the very beginning of the war. Presidency of the Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina. Cvijetin Simic, pursuant to his authority, issues this order prohibiting the carrying of weapons in public by persons not in uniform and unauthorised persons. It says: Persons -- it says un-uniformed and unauthorised persons are hereby prohibited from carrying weapons without a permit in public within the territory of Bijeljina municipality and it envisions certain sanctions in case of violation.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about this order. It helped me when I came there. We enforced it, because many un-uniformed people carried ammunition belts, wore ammunition belts and carried even rifles. There were even psychiatric patients whom I had known from before carrying weapons, going about town, and it was pursuant to this order that we were able to disarm them, take them to the misdemeanour court, and I think this order had a very good effect in the town of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have to clear up one thing for the sake of precision. When you mention the Crisis Staff, do you make a distinction between the Presidency of the municipality, the Territorial Defence Staff, and the Crisis Staff? You see, on the 8th of April, Bijeljina does not have a Crisis Staff any more. It has a Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you know that the Presidency in Bijeljina was established already in April and was operative, but there was a Crisis Staff that operated where the leading people in the municipality met and made key decisions. I don't know what that body was called. All I know is that the head of the Crisis Staff was Mauzer, and he was also a deputy to the Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina. He was not a member of the Crisis Staff, but he was the chairman of the personnel commission, I think. But when certain decisions and restructuring were done regarding the Crisis Staff, he took over the functions of the Crisis Staff, replacing Cvijetin Simic, and he didn't let Cvijetin Simic do any of that. He wanted to do it himself. I don't know exactly how he did it, but I heard from people that he arrogated all this authority very brutally, and for a year or so he acted as the head of the Crisis Staff, as person number one in Bijeljina who was able to make any sort of decision, do whatever he wanted without being afraid of any punishment or even being confronted by anyone. And I see that there are, on the other hand, very useful orders such as this one prohibiting the carrying of weapons in public, helping to restore law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1438, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this context I'm just wondering why the previous one was put under seal, because that's not -- not different from what -- what we have here from the former. It's a decision, so why would it be under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you help us in this regard, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quite understand what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff is saying, because this passage that I didn't want to be seen has not been translated. The English version, in any case, does not have to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, we'll put it in the public domain. Yes. We admit it publicly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder, I thought this, what we have, the English translation would be reflecting the B/C/S document, but then I hear there is something not translated. I'm just wondering what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Was it the case or you just wanted not to broadcast the document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second part, the untranslated one, refers to a different decision about an appointment, and it's not an integral part. It's not organically linked with this first order. If we go into private session briefly, I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3621, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we have to be very precise in terms of admitting that document. You need to redact the unnecessary part from the Serbian version then. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus on this. In Bijeljina, at the session of the Municipal Assembly, which is working on the 10th of April, the Presidency of the Municipal Assembly made a decision to amend the decision on the names of squares and streets in the town of Bijeljina and the settlements of Janja and Dvorovi. Take a look at this and I'll put this proposition to you: Certain streets are renamed because they had been named by Partisans or Chetniks or whatever, Communist regime, and they are renamed to remove these Communist names. Let's see what happens with Muslim names. Number 4, Hamze Hamzic Street shall be renamed Mehmeda Spaho street. So one Muslim name is being replaced by another Muslim name, correct? Is that right? Is it right that Hamze Hamzic Street, who was Muslim, probably a partisan fighter, is renamed Mehmeda Spaho Street; right? And both of them were Muslims. It's not on the transcript. Can we have an answer from you? Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, streets were renamed, but they were renamed into the names of Muslims who were suitable in the eyes of Serbs. For instance, the street called Jaksic Brothers, was renamed into Second Lieutenant Smajic Street. Second Lieutenant Smajic got killed fighting for the Serbian Army in Vukovar. That's how they wanted to acknowledge the fact. Then the street you mentioned, Hamze Hamzic Street, I can't see how it was renamed. Mehmed Spaho. You know who Mehmed Spaho was and what role he played in the Second World War. So all of these are streets that were an eyesore to the Muslim people, and they still want these streets to be renamed again because there was the street that was renamed into Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me put it to you that's my case, Mehmed Spaho was the leader of a pro-Yugoslav Muslim organisation. His name is given to the street previously called Hamze Hamzic who was a Communist. Then Fadil Jahic Spaniard Street, a fighter in the Spanish civil war, is renamed into the name of the member of the young Bosnia organisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, slow down and start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So number 7, Brothers Jaksic street is renamed into Second Lieutenant Smajic street, a Muslim who got killed in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Jaksic Brothers, were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Point 9. Ivan Markovic, Irishman Street is renamed Hasan Kikic. Ivan Markovic Irishman is a Serb, whereas Hasan Kikic is a Muslim, an author.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Point 12. Patris Lumumba street, a leader of Angola, is renamed into Camil Sijerica street, Camil Sijeric being a famous author?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Alija Alijagic street, and Alija Alijagic was a Communist and an assassin of a minister before the war --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minister Draskovic in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- is renamed into Meso Selimovic, a great writer of Muslim origin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see the next page. 21, the name Muslim Brigades --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, while you're complaining about the shortage of time, I'm struggling to see the point of reading out all these names. What's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, the war had already started, and in the renaming of streets there is nothing discriminatory or ethnic. It is all about politics. The names of Muslim Communists are replaced by the names of Muslim intellectuals, writers, authors, people whose value is less transitory. The point is that the authorities in Bijeljina are making changes not on an ethnic basis but an ideological basis, without removing Muslim names. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please spare us your comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. You can put your question simply, in a simpler manner, but reading out all these streets names was pointless. That was my point. Yes, since you've heard the accused, you are entitled to answer, Mr. Davidovic. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You should not deprive me of my right to comment. If streets were renamed, I must tell you that some streets were renamed four times during the war and some of these names have been completely eliminated. It's true that Muslim names were sometimes given to Serbian streets with the aim of acknowledging people who were taking the Serbian side, who were somehow suitable to the Serbian spirit. You know who Meso Selimovic is. All these people were close to the Serbian people and who supported the Serbian people in their literary or other work. But Muslims never accepted the new names of these streets and they still challenge them and they still demand that streets be renamed back and that Meso Selimovic and Hasan Kikic and this lieutenant what's-his-name who replaced Jaksic brothers be removed because these names irritate the Muslims. Why were these names given in the first place because it was effective vis-a-vis the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at point 21. Muslim Brigades Street - and Muslim Brigades was a Partisan Communist brigade - is just renamed Muslim Street. And my case is that this is about ideology, not about ethnicity. Those were pro-Yugoslav Muslims, and the Serbian side wants and supports pro-Yugoslav Muslims. It's their right. And the Muslims who were either anti-Yugoslav or Communist were removed as street names.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This street that you say was renamed Muslim Street was renamed again a couple of months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the name of one Muslim replaced by the name of another Muslim? That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please bear in mind the invaluable advice given Judge Baird. Put your question one by one, if you would like to get the answer, if at all. So this question was whether one Muslim name was replaced by another Muslim name. Is that your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. My question was whether the reason for these changes was ideological or ethnic, when the Muslim street names were removed or was that something that went along with the change of the system and a change of the favourites. The Serbs favoured pro-Yugoslav Muslims and Muslim authors rather than the Muslim revolutionaries. Was Hasan Kikic both revolutionary and a writer, but he was more a writer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. My question is whether he was a well-known writer and that it was more important that he was a writer than that he was a revolutionary?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a writer. Meso Selimovic was also a writer. Ivo Andric is a writer as well but the Muslim population did not see him as their writer; that's the problem. He is a writer and we rightfully treated him as one but the Muslim population did not accept him, for the reason that they thought that it was at the detriment of the Muslim people. That was the reason why I'm saying this. It was all calculated to change names, to rename the streets after Muslims again, but people who had sympathies for the Serbs. You know why Meso Selimovic moved into Belgrade and you know about the murder of his brother, so let me not talk about this background information. You know that all that was calculated to irritate Muslims in this way, by letting them know who were the Muslims who can be acceptable for the Serbs, those who were inclined to us. I'm not going to say that writers were obeying us, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, Meso Selimovic is really a big writer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in item 21, it says the Muslim Brigade Street change into Muslim Street. So who doesn't like the Muslim Street?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know how long it remained the Muslim Street? They removed the name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted? I wonder they did not remove them all. Perhaps we should have named streets after the Muslims who were Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, please. And don't ascribe to me something I never said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1439, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3622, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, this is also a decision from the meeting of the Presidency of the Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina, dated the 14th of April, on the appointment of commission for enrolling children into the first grade of primary school. Number one primary school Muhamed Mehmedbasic in Bijeljina. Did you know that one of the schools was called Muhamed Mehmedbasic and that he was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear about the name of this school and it is the first time that I see that that was the name it had. I never heard it or came across that that there was a school with such a name in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please have a look at item number 2. Fatima Odzakovic was an employee. She was a children's psychologist at this school.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but she was removed from office and left from the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They wrote to us about this several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see the next page please. Under item 5, Primary School Meso Selimovic in Janja. Psychologist teacher Jasarevic, Dzana; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see under item 6, Dzana Jasarevic was a children's psychologist at another school in Glavicica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was just one class in Glavicica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this Dzana also a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the next page just to see that it was signed by Cvijetin Simic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just tell me what date was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 14th of April, 1992. So it was in the middle of the war.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the outbreak of the war. They were appointed on the 14th of April. Were they still there in September when the school year began?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please let us stick to the subject.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask for this to be admitted now, and I will present another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1440, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 8276, please. Can we please have 1D3623, because I cannot identify the date here. So we don't need this one. 1D3623, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a decision on maintaining law and order in Bijeljina. Cvijetin Simic once again. The 28th of April, 1992, and item 1 talks about maintaining law and order and that that can be done only by members of active duty and reserve police. In item 2, setting up local check-points in local communes is prohibited and carrying out the said duties by civilians and other unauthorised persons. Would you agree that this is also the implementation of law and order rather than implementing chaos?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A decision about public law and order existed even before this one. Something was changed in certain items, among other things that it was prohibited to set up check-points in villages and the decision on public law and order and the security of traffic existed in the territory of the municipality even before this was adopted. So this was not the first decision relating to public law and order that was adopted. As far as I was in the police there, such a decision existed and I was responsible for its implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, why are you trying to devalue this? Of course it existed, but then Simic was giving support to that, and you arrested people on the basis of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Even if he hadn't, we would be acting in accordance with the previous decision. So there is nothing contested about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted and have another document before the break? Can this be admitted, please, 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We mark it for identification again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3624, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 29th of May, same gentleman, Cvijetin Simic who is still president of the presidency of the Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina. Would you agree this is a conclusion the presidency of the Bijeljina municipality is of the view that the armed and uniformed groups and individuals who have come to the area of Bijeljina from elsewhere and without an invitation by the legal authorities of Bijeljina municipality act in a manner which gives rise to the violations of public law and order and endangers the security situation. In this connection, the Presidency prohibits any engagement of any individual or group in any other capacity in the organs of internal affairs or the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as legal authorities, instructors or any other capacity. Would you agree that in this way the Presidency of the Bijeljina also tried to defend itself from incursions by various persons who were armed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, but when I came there in the month of June, I found Pejo, who was Arkan's deputy in SUP and one Sasa who was a komandir of the police station. He had that duty and held that position. And the other one had the insignia of chief inspector, just as I did. The decision was adopted in May. I arrived in June, and I found him carrying out the duty of the commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just another question, Mr. Davidovic. If they could implement their decisions through their police, would you have been invited?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you something frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, please allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are trying to slander this leadership. You said that they liked the chaos. You see that they didn't. If they could have implemented this decision without you would you have arrived at all?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I arrived with 15 men. What can 15 men do in such a big area? You did not ask me how come that you came with 15 men and you did what you did in Brcko, Bijeljina, and Zvornik. Bijeljina could have done that. It did not need the federal SUP, nor did anyone have to come to help it disarm paramilitaries. It had legal institutions, organs and the police which was professionally trained so they could do that. When I arrived I contacted the active duty policemen whom I knew. I told them to do what was in accordance with the law and I allowed them to do that. I didn't allow anyone to beat them, slap them across the face. When they had this support for me as a police superior, the police really started doing its work and public law and order was imposed in the town. Fifteen men did not need to come there. It was a small unit that did that. You didn't ask me how I managed to do that with 15 men. I didn't do it with 15 men. I engaged active duty police then from Bijeljina, from Brcko and from Zvornik and I managed to reinstitute the legal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Davidovic, did Mico Stanisic place Karisik and members of his unit at your disposal and give you authority to call for reinforcement from Brcko and from Zvornik? Were you able on the basis of this authority given to you by Minister Stanisic to enlarge the units and to implement all this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I asked Mr. Stanisic not to give me Karisik or his help. I was afraid of Karisik's unit. I believed them to be unprofessional and incompetent, and this unit was not sufficiently efficient to do this work. At the insistence of Minister Stanisic, I accepted the unit but I gave them peripheral duties that had to do with dealing with the Yellow Wasps. What proved that I was right was that when I left Zvornik for Belgrade, this unit which was headed by Karisik was let me not the same as the Yellow Wasps but it had similar impact on the population as the Yellow Wasps. They continued bringing into Muslim apartments, seize them, live in them so they violated public law and order and they also had serious problems with them just like when the Yellow Wasps were in power.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted and, Mr. Davidovic, none of that is true. We'll prove that. It was a high profile and elite unit and you used it. Can it be admitted, please, and then we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, I'm asking you this: Whether the authorities for whom you say in the paragraph that we referred to wanted to have chaos? Were they trying to have law and order or chaos?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what happened once that we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wait. These authorities, this one is an active supporter of the Prosecution. I'm trying to ask you whether they were trying to implement law and order and that you were invited on the basis of that, but you're saying, Yes, but. You say, Yes, but.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to testify, Mr. Karadzic? Refrain from making comments, and please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, you at the very beginning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I observed that the witness tried to answer twice now and he was basically shouted down. This is what I'm actually observing. I think that should not be allowed, that he's basically shouting the witness down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. I think it's a perfect time to take a break. We'll break for an hour. We'll deal with matters when we come -- yes Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I indicated I would respond to the court about the reply and the timing the Court indicated it had would like us to have it in, by the end of the day. If the end of the day means close of business at 4.00 that would be difficult, but if it means sometime today, I think we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would be appreciated. There's one further matter. It may be better to be known at this moment. On the day before yesterday, i.e., 28th of June, the Chamber admitted the associate exhibit tendered through Mr. Milorad Davidovic with the exception of 14 statements which were listed in footnote 144 of his amalgamated statement and for which it indicated that a decision would be issued in due course. The Chamber has decided that these 14 statements would not be admitted into evidence on the basis of the established practice that when it comes to the statements of third parties, unless a witness comments on and confirms or adopts the content of that statement, the third party statement would not be admitted through that witness. We'll rise and adjourn for an hour, resume at 1.40. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to today's timing for the witness, I would mention that I would have about 20 minutes to half an hour of redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Excuse me, can this previous document 1D3624 be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I'll try, because I'm pressed for time, to put to you as briefly as I can documents about the attempts to enforce law and order just before you came to Bijeljina. 1D3625, please. This will show why you were invited. 1D3625. This first order, at the top I believe it's been translated, 11 June, Cvijetin Simic as president of the Municipal Presidency issues an order, and ex officio, he's chairman of the Defence board of the municipality. The order is to place under single -- under the single command of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina all armed units. Does this order indicate that this had been a problem?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3628.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 25 June, perhaps one or two days before you arrived the same Mr. Simic, president of the Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina passes this conclusion which means the Assembly had convened and adopted this conclusion: "To uphold the decision of the government and the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to send Special Police Units or a Special Police Unit to Bijeljina to protect law and order in co-operation with the Bijeljina public security station in keeping with the regulation," and so on and so forth. Is this another preparatory step for this major operation of restoring order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this conclusion. I didn't know it had been adopted, but obviously it had.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1444, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3629, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 25 June, pursuant to the previous conclusion, the president of the Municipal Assembly now issues an order: "Prohibiting uniformed and armed persons from moving in public in Bijeljina unless authorised," et cetera. "All armed and uniformed persons whose presence in public is not in accordance with this order are hereby to be removed from all public places in the municipality of Bijeljina." Is it what the order says?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the gist.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this 1D3629 will be admitted as Exhibit D1445.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, please P1478. It's a typed page in English, 220, and in Serbian it's a typed page, 218.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are diary entries, entries in the diary of General Mladic. We can move forward, perhaps, to earlier pages to see that it's the 23rd of June, just before you came. P1478. I could like to see the typed version, Serbian typed version pages 218, and the English typed version is page 220. We can see that it's 23rd of June at 6.00 p.m. Yes. The page is 217. He notes down what I said: "Karadzic: The following people are to go to Bijeljina tomorrow, Plavsic, Krajisnik, Mladic, Subotic, Gvero, Tolimir. " Next, I say: "Two groups of paramilitary units are active in Semberija (Mauzer's and Blagojevic's) groups. They are very extreme. "All units must be placed under the single command of the army and the police." Next bullet point: "In Bijeljina try to resolve the problem politically. They must not suspend the civilian authorities." To the best of your knowledge were the civilian authorities in the entire region including Zvornik and Bijeljina threatened by the presence of these armed groups?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were. I believe in Semberija those authorities were completely suspended because Mauzer had taken over completely as president, as commander, as anything and everything and nobody was able to confront him. I'm talking about Mauzer, whose real name is Savic. Now, as far as Blagojevic is concerned, my answer would be a little different, and I believe it needs clarifying. His role needs clarifying, but only if you want me to. I believe this reflects the real situation in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But to assist you, we agree, don't we, that Blagojevic was a more positive character. He protected Muslims, did not arrest them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this would require a slightly broader answer, if the Trial Chamber allows. Mirko Blagojevic at the outset was one of the people who was part of this organisation, and then he transferred to Seselj's Radical Party. With the beginning of the war, there occurred a flash -- a clash between Mauzer and Blagojevic on personal grounds because Mauzer tried to subordinate Blagojevic and to place Blagojevic's units under his own command. Blagojevic refused. So at one point Blagojevic imposed a complete blockade on Bijeljina, putting roadblocks on all access roads, and of their own accord and self-will they arrested Mauzer, kept him in a cellar, beating him. I was around and General Gracanin gave me a call at the time and told me that together with Pero Mihajlovic I should go to Bijeljina and see what it's all about, to try to resolve this problem, to prevent conflicts between Serbs. I came there. I found those roadblocks. At the moment when I entered the SUP building Mauzer came to -- had come to the SUP a few minutes before me. He had obviously been beaten. He had managed to escape that basement somehow, and that conflict dates back to that time. Well, at the time I came to the SUP, the entire municipal leadership was there, and they were discussing precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree I could not have sent a stronger delegation to Bijeljina, Plavsic, vice-president; Krajisnik, speaker of the Assembly; Mladic; Subotic, et cetera? Don't you agree that these were people of authority, a very strong delegation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those people had the authority to deal with the problem if it could be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see English page 313 and Serbian 311, also from the Mladic diaries, where he notes what I said. It says: "Karadzic: Regarding Muslims and Croats, we are going to build a state with a rule of law, not an ethnically pure one." The typed version, 311. Serbian typed version, 311. The English page is good. We are looking at the English page. Do you agree that it's not a protest, it's a serious meeting discussing serious subjects?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll continue. We'll continue with these preparations to deal with lawlessness. Let's see how things -- what things looked like a bit later. 1D2751, please. Do you agree -- I believe there is a translation. Do you agree this is a telegram from me to the Ministry of the Interior of 29 April 1994? I'm saying the Main Staff had informed me that in several municipalities, Teslic, Petrovo, Knezevo, Vogosca, Ilijas, attempts were being made to set up paramilitary units? And in the last paragraph I say it's necessary for the organs of the Ministry of the Interior to get involved in exposing and preventing these activities. "All offenders should be sanctioned, and I need to be kept advised of this." Do you agree that's what I wrote to the minister?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it concerns fighting paramilitaries following a report from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1446, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 65 ter 13357.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the same day I replied to the Main Staff, personally to General Mladic, saying that I had ordered the Ministry of the Interior to put in place these measures?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 29 April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1447, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3783, please. I don't know if there is a translation. There is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree on the same day the security advisor, on the authority of the president and invoking the order of the Main Staff, requires Petrovo municipality - and there is a similar document sent to other municipalities - to report, and it says that what's going on there runs counter to the order of the president to disarm paramilitary units, and they require the municipalities to urgently inform the president of the measures taken.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. It's the same kind of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Davidovic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit D1448.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that information about the legal troubles of your son was a media affair and that it had something to do with your testimony in Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After that, the Trial Chamber refused to admit those newspaper articles and told me to show something else if I have it. Can I now call up 1D3800. We gave an order yesterday to our investigators to collect evidence, and we have this evidence now before us. It has just arrived today, but I'll read it because we have no translation. The district prosecutor's office of Bijeljina. I'll read it slowly. Number such and such, 30th June.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would actually oppose using this document on the grounds of relevancy. If I can see it here, it relates to not the witness but the witness's son, and looking at the numbers, it seems to be matters from 2007, 2006. I don't really see that there's any relevance to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, can you help us in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have to note with regret that this witness very carelessly involved both his son and my family in his allegations, saying that his legal troubles resulted from his testimony in Krajisnik, and in paragraph 205, he states that his son was kidnapped, and that is also somehow connected, and he levies very serious allegations against prominent officials of the MUP of Republika Srpska, and of course he associates that with his testimony in Krajisnik. I am very reluctant to deal with this, but this goes to credibility and the essence of his evidence. We now see that this has nothing to do with Krajisnik. The first criminal report was in 1993, and there have been eight judgements in total up until 2005.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I would not like to enter into polemics with you. My son is an adult, 40 years old. He bears responsibility for his own behaviour. I'll say something else. When his name is mentioned in newspaper stories and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He wasn't asking a question yet to you. He addressed me. Mr. Karadzic, I think I told you we exhausted this issue yesterday. Move on to another topic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Excellency, you said I shouldn't bring newspaper articles, but if I have something new, I should show it. This goes to credibility. The witness associated the troubles of his son with his own testimony, which is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Davidovic, out of these eight judgements, were five before 2005?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. Just a second. I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber does not see the significant relevance of this document. Please move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, will paragraph 205 be excluded from the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, after Bijeljina and Brcko, you were invited by the local leadership to help resolve the crisis in Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You testified about that also in Belgrade in the trial of Branko Grujic and others from Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D3793, please. It's the transcript of your testimony in Zvornik -- I mean Belgrade, concerning the Zvornik case. Is it true that in Zvornik once again you concluded that the civilian authorities had no real power or ability to confront these people?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said at the beginning. When we arrived, they were completely sidelined, and this group of Yellow Wasps had placed those authorities, leadership, under their command and did whatever they wanted. When they had done the job they had been paid for, then they turned into their own opposites.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see page 4 in Serbian and 5 in English. It's the last third in English, the last fourth in Serbian. You say at all entry points in Zvornik they had their check-points. They had their own men. They had full control over everything going on in Zvornik. And you say the authorities had no power. They were able to beat up policemen and anyone else; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now see Serbian page 5, English 6. You say Jekic, Zugic, and you think Popovic came to see you. Jekic was from the MUP of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Zugic is the Goran Zugic who, as you confirmed, was killed in Podgorica and had served in the state security in Podgorica and then moved to the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He moved to Zvornik to work for the state security there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This Popovic was also a member of the Secret Service, but he hid that and stayed in Zvornik under a false name.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't a member of the Secret Service. He pretended to be, and he used a false name, but when I checked through the service to see whether he indeed belonged to the security service, whether somebody had sent him, I was unable to confirm that, and nobody in fact intervened for him on any issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serbian 6, English 7, please. You confirmed on this page towards the top, the second third, that with Colonel Salapura and Karisik, who was a police general, which you did not mention here, you made a plan in which everybody was assigned a key task and Zvornik was cut off from Vlasenica. You had to cross a bridge to go to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It's not correct. Karisik did not participate in planning or this operation. He was involved as a member of the special unit he led, but he wasn't involved in the planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I have to read: "Together with me, Petar Salapura was involved in the staff. He was a lieutenant-colonel or a colonel of the VRS. He was in the command together with me. He planned and organised this operation."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "There was a special unit of the MUP led by Karisik."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There was a special unit. This Petar Salapura was involved in the planning, in all the details, but Karisik did not. His unit only participated in the liberation of Zvornik from paramilitary units. I'll tell you why you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't have time. Let me just read what you said. It's all about precision. Perhaps you did not make this error deliberately. "Milenko Karisik and I had an elaborate plan with detailed assignments," et cetera. So Milenko Karisik participated in the planning?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't. He had an assignment. I just told him what his assignment was in that plan. He didn't participate in the planning, and he didn't know the whole plan. He use knew his own mission in that population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did the -- did you say in that transcript "Karisik and I had an elaborate plan"? Could you read that part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I read or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That operation, there was a special unit of the MUP led by Milenko Karisik, and we had an elaborate plan. We had an elaborate plan that means, where everyone got a detailed assignment what and where they are supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Jekic came to see you to ask your assistance in disarming them.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, twice or thrice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: English page 7 -- sorry, 8. He described what they were doing in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see Serbian page 10, English 13. You say when you made the arrests and neutralised this large group of 100 to 150 paramilitaries, Branko Grujic, president of the municipality -- or, rather, the temporary government of Zvornik, couldn't believe it. He even cried from joy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's English page 13, straddling 14. Thank you. He couldn't believe it. He asked you several times, "Is it really true they were arrested?"

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he said, "Will they be released?" One woman who was on that staff was from Sekovici, married to some doctor in Zvornik. I knew her name. I forgot it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now see page 17, then 18 in English and Serbian 14. I'm confused Mr. Davidovic, because in Belgrade you said, "When I arrested them, I knew it. I took statements from them." Whereas yesterday you told us somebody else took those statements.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doesn't it say here, "When I arrested them, I knew. I took statements from them."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrested them and brought them to Bijeljina, a group of crime inspectors was set up located in offices interviewing several people, taking statements. As far as I was able to, I took the time to visit all these offices, to listen for a while to these interviews and hear what the arrested men were saying. So I didn't spend a lot of time on all of it, but I wanted to follow all this work, to be kept informed about what the service was doing, so I visited those interviews for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: English page 22. That's where you describe how it happened. The Yellow Wasps were not always called Yellow Wasps. They had a different name in the outset. They were volunteers. They went to the front line. When they got fed up with it, they came back to urban areas and established control there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serbian, it's page 17 and 18, English 22. Then English page -- sorry, Serbian 19, and English page 23, the last paragraph, then on to page 24. You said here and there that Batkovic camp had been formed by the municipality as a labour camp.
