utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the same thing as here. Before the decision was issued to appoint the camp commander, the army had first approached the General Dencic, and that was later confirmed by Colonel Ilic, and they asked for premises for a facility where some sort of labour camp or a collection centre for Muslims would be placed. The municipality asked an enterprise called Semberija, and this enterprise told them they could use their facility in Batkovic where this company had one of its facilities, agricultural facilities, large barns, large hangars where they kept agricultural machinery. They had large plots of land. It was their farm. And the municipality then suggested to the army and gave its approval that the army may use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that somebody misinformed you? Batkovic was a legal and legitimate camp for prisoners of war, not for Muslims who did not respond to call-up, as it says on page 24 in English and 19 in Serbian. It was legitimate, and it was the only central prison for prisoners of war from which persons were exchanged. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning when the camp in Batkovic was established, persons were brought there from Brezevo Polje, also some persons from Zvornik, and some from Bijeljina. Later on when people found out about this, because at first no one spoke about Batkovic in public, and I remember the press conference that was held on that day in Bijeljina when we arrested the Yellow Wasps. That is when a large group of some 50-odd journalists came from Belgrade, from Serbia, and they asked whether it was true there was some camp called Batkovic somewhere, and they asked whether I knew about that. I was answering the journalists' questions then, and I realised that that was the first time they started putting serious questions about this camp. Later on when this camp was taken over by the military and, as I said, it was people from Brezevo Polje, Brcko and Bijeljina that were kept there, also people from Zvornik, Janja, et cetera, these persons were taken from there to labour on Majevica, in the Semberija company, also in some companies like the construction company Rad and so on. They took them there and brought them back, and later on this camp or -- well, this labour camp as they called it, grew into a camp for prisoners of war. I did not know that prisoners of war were kept there. I did not realise that that was how it was defined later, that such persons were brought there, but I do know that the International Red Cross came later and that one knew who the persons there were kept and how many were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1776 65 ter. I need to call that up. It's not on the list, but due to this answer of yours I have to ask for this document. 11776. This is a document of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. It's got to have a translation, I think, because it's a 65 ter document, and instructions are being provided here concerning the organisation of life and work at Ekonomija, and everything is prescribed there, what people do, when they go out for a walk, everything. Just look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this was a camp for prisoners of war. As for any proof of it being something else, do you have any proof?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of facts and I speak about facts, and I know people who were there and who had work obligations who went there and came back and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since there is no translation I will have to read out at least the first paragraph. It says: "On the order of the commander of the East Bosnia Corps, strictly confidential," et cetera, et cetera, "the instructions on the treatment of imprisoned persons number," et cetera, et cetera, "on the 13th of June, 1992, the ministry of the defence of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and regulations concerning International Law of War, I hereby prescribe this instruction on the organisation of life and work in the camp and the rights and obligations of persons who are prisoners there." Do you see anything here that would be in contravention of the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I said that I knew about this when I came to Bijeljina because Colonel Ilic told me that in Batkovic there is this camp, that the commander of that camp was appointed and that the function of this camp was determined by the corps command. I would like to say something to you that is not included in these instructions here. Actually, beforehand, they came to different facilities looking for something that would be a proper location for this kind of camp. It wasn't only Batkovic. They had a few options, and they visited them, and they even thought it would be near Ugljevik, near the mine there, and then other places were considered too. While this procedure was underway for this to be a collection camp in Batkovic, a fence was being built, also a door. Where the machines were, they put up a door so that it could be closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page. Item 10. Actually, on the top of this page it says, "Valuables, money, and other personal property of value can be temporarily taken away and returned when persons are dismissed from the camp ...," and so on. And then item 10 says: "A list of persons kept in this camp concerning their personal details shall be submitted to the Red Cross of the municipality of Bijeljina with a view to provide the information to their relatives and to the International Red Cross. The persons who are kept prisoner have to be treated humanely and violence should not be applied against them. Exceptionally, if the prescribed order is disrupted, then measures of force may be applied." And also there's a reference to the entry of unauthorised persons. Do you agree that these instructions were written up in accordance with the norms of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Despot, the first commander of the camp compiled these instructions. He was appointed by the military. He was a lieutenant-colonel. He lived in Nis. I know him personally, and I personally discussed this with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1449, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next item, Mr. Tieger, I have just noted that a motion was filed in relation to the next witness asking for a reconsideration. We would be benefitted if we could have your response by the end of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I've been in communication about that, Your Honour. That may be -- well, it will be difficult. Of course we'll try to do it, but I wouldn't at this point want to preclude the possibility of the Prosecution having to respond orally at the beginning of the day tomorrow, but we'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3793. We're going back to that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're going back to the transcript of your testimony in Belgrade. Is it correct that this Djurkovic had his counterpart or partner on the Muslim side and that they were some kind of a commission for exchanging civilians and family reunification?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, on the other side there was also a person that co-ordinated the work of these groups -- or, rather, the exchange of persons. This is a man who is a lawyer. I think his name is -- now, was it Bakir Pasic or -- I cannot remember right now. There's so many names in my head. I think that it is Bakir Pasic. He was born in Bijeljina. There was full co-operation with him when persons were being exchanged through institutions. Then lists were provided to Djurkovic. That is to say persons that should be brought over for exchanges, because there were some who asked through persons like Bakir to be brought in and then taken to Tuzla, and in return Djurkovic asked for other persons of Serb ethnicity be brought there and then exchanged. These were contacts that they managed themselves without involving persons who were in detention or in prison or the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, these were not prisoners of war but civilians and their family members. Is it correct that this Bakir gave this wish list of the Muslims, which ones they wanted in Tuzla, and then he got from Vojkan the wish list of the Serbs, which are the Serbs they want from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that. People would say get my mother, get my father, et cetera, and then Djurkovic would say in return, "Bring me such and such a person who was in the territory of Tuzla." And that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Serbian it's page 20 and in English 25 and 26. They collected money for these services; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I cannot be certain, but that's what I assume. Nothing was done free of charge in that war. Everything had a price.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's Serbian page 21 and English 26. And you say that the Serbs either from Batkovic or elsewhere were taken towards Brcko or Ban Brdo in the territory of Majevica. They would take them off buses and have them exchanged; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would take them out of buses and if it was at Ban Brdo and Majevica then they would be released and then they walked down a road because that's where the separation line was, and then as they get close to this zone where the Muslim forces are sometimes there would be shooting, random gunfire, and then they'd wait there for a while and sometimes they would be taken by trucks to Brcko and then they'd go to the separation line near Rahic. Again they would be released, crossed the line kept by the Serb forces, and then they crossed the lines to the Muslim forces and that is how they exchanged them. Well, I mean they didn't exchange them. That's how they took them. Exchanges took place later in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 21 in Serbian, 26 in English, you mentioned that there was some agency, some tourist agency within the SUP where you could legally apply, give 2.500, hand over a passport ten days in advance and in the amalgamated statement you corrected yourself and you said it wasn't in the MUP but that the MUP -- sorry. Actually, on page 21, have a look at it. Within SUP it was established, or rather, a travel agency was established. Actually, it was another witness who said where it was and that it was legal. Legally people would apply, pay, hand over their passport and then travel abroad; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was this organisation attached to the SUP or whatever, but I know that Kovac gave his consent at the time to the effect that Muslims who wanted to leave certainly had to pay from 2.500 to 5.000 marks. Some were actually staying at a hotel waiting for a certain group to be established, then contact would be established with the MUP of Serbia. At that point in time, it was Puzovic who was head of the border department and then co-operation would be established and an agreement would be reached as to how many buses should be there. Then Vojkan Djurkovic would head that column, take over these persons and sometimes escort them with police cars to Sentilj. No, not Sentilj, Horgos, on the Hungarian border near Subotica and then they'd take them to our border. They would check their passports. They would let them go towards Hungary. The Hungarians didn't want to take them in, and then between the two borders a group of buses would spend a day or two or three there until the Red Cross arrived, took them over and then put them up in different countries in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 29 Serbian, 37 English, you call these persons who you arrested dogs of war. Do you still stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is a name used for person who go wherever there is a war in order to be able to loot. They stop at nothing. They only pursue their own interests and they find it in looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You repeated on page 40 in Serbian, 51 English, that you were asked to come on the basis of the conversation at that took place between Panic and Karadzic. That is the Yugoslav Prime Minister Panic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Everything I said here as well. That is what I was told at the time, that it was at your request at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 41 now in Serbian, 52 in English, it says the Presiding Judge is asking you did you know that later on proceedings were stopped against these persons? This is a reference to the Yellow Wasps. They were no longer in detention, and the proceedings were suspended. "Answer: No, I just know that they were released from detention and I know what happened to Vuckovic. I was with my unit in Pljevlja at the time ...," et cetera. So you said that you did not know at that point in time that proceedings had been stopped but you did know that they were released from detention?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I never said that proceedings against them were stopped. I've been saying throughout that proceedings were against them, but they were actually in detention for 30 days and then released. I see that this document in front of me Serbia is asking for a continuation of proceedings and so on. However, these proceedings were never brought to an end in Bosnia. Information was sought, and the proceedings stopped at that point because these persons went to Serbia and never came back. Although they actually did come back. They did cross the border. They did come to Zvornik and Bijeljina, but these proceedings were not completed. It was only later on the basis of what you said yourself and on the basis of information gathered by the Republic of Serbia through their subsequent activities. They came to learn that crimes had been committed and then proceedings were instituted much later in Sabac on the basis of the information that they had had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were the Vuckovic brothers arrested?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sabac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You arrested them; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not I personally, but Dragan Andan and three other members of the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then the proposal was -- actually, Sabac is in Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The proposal was to have them transported to Bosnia while their followers were arrested in Zvornik itself, Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. They were in Zvornik all day long until late at night, but they were afraid of being arrested. And during the night they would cross the Drina River and spend the night there. I was not aware of that. As I was preparing to carry out this operation, Jekic came to see me and said to me, inter alia, I'm offering you this possibility to arrest Zuco and Repic, because during the night they are not in Bosnia. And I asked how come he knew, and he said I know they're in Sabac and I'm offering this to you. You can arrest them in Sabac, in Serbia, and you can bring them to Bosnia. I accepted to look into that, and then I was told that I would be given this possibility of arresting them, taking them to Bosnia, and then he said and then we would arrest them and in this way kill them and close the page regarding these fools. I actually violated this agreement, because proceedings were underway after I arrested them. In Serbia, they didn't even know about this when this proposal was made, along with a criminal report three days later, I received -- well, not exactly threats, but I was criticised. They were asking what I had done. They wanted to get me there. They wanted me -- they wanted to make me do something illegal, and then they would say, Uh-huh, now you have to do what we tell you to do. I managed to save myself. I did not do anything that would be held against me later. However, this was held against me in Serbia, and I had very serious problems because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us focus on page 43 in Serbian and 54/55 in English. In Davidovic just now described this offer to have them arrested in Serbia, brought over to Bosnia -- or, rather, Republika Srpska, and be liquidated there, and they ask you why. You explain why. Let me ask you, Mr. Davidovic, were you sorry about me as the president of the country in which one Pavlovic or Popovic and one Jekic were doing what they wanted and wondering whether they would arrest or liquidate someone in the country that I was responsible for?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say, Mr. Karadzic, that as president you had great responsibility at the time, but I reflected about this frequently, whether you knew all this or whether you couldn't prevent it, but objectively speaking, there was great chaos. And how was it possible that you didn't manage to find associates who were trusted men, who were able, and who were willing to do everything in accordance with the law, because I see that you insisted on these legal measures. I must say that up until today or yesterday, I didn't know that you wrote so many orders and requested that legal measures be taken, and your name was always mentioned in any context. Whatever anyone did, he always claimed to have the approval of President Karadzic. Krajisnik or Karadzic were those who decided. I did reflect about this and I must admit that sometimes I wondered why did he invite us to come over when all that was happening and taking place? I tried to be, let me not say realistic, but I was thinking as a professional how was it possible that no one did what we had to do, because it was nothing that required special -- a special level of professionalism. It's a daily job for the police. You just have to be decisive enough and professionally capable of doing it properly, if they had your support. And I see through all this they could have had your support, so they shouldn't have been afraid of possible consequences of such activities. If I had known of this support, I would have returned from Serbia to the MUP and I would have placed myself at your disposal, and you may be sure that you wouldn't be sitting here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You had, in addition to your 15 men, another 300 men at your disposal from the army, from Salapura and from Stanisic from police; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a significant armed group, and when we entered Zvornik that implied combat activities. That is to say, we fired shots, they were shooting at us. Someone could have gotten killed on either side, but fortunately, no one got wounded. And I must say we used more chemical weapons to chase them out of apartments and houses and in this way we arrested them. So we prevented any killings in the shoot-out between us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please slow down and note how your question was reflected in the transcript and please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It has not been recorded. You are right when you said that I said that Mr. Davidovic, in addition to his 15 men, had at his disposal from our police and our army an additional number of up to 300 men and you arrested a total of almost 200 men, about 180 members of the Yellow Wasps; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just need to clarify the number of 300 men. When I went to Bosnia, primarily to Bijeljina, I knew what people I would have at my disposal in Bijeljina. I also knew some of the people in Brcko, primarily, I have in mind the active duty policemen. And when, in addition to my 15 men, I would have 50 or 60 professionally trained policemen from Bijeljina, a part of the military police from Bijeljina, I would also have the support of people in Zvornik who were also active duty policemen. I had a military unit which was sent by the Main Staff and Karisik's unit, numbering 150 men. I was then certain that they couldn't slip away or put up such resistance that we would have to withdraw. I knew that we could carry out this task and this is why I had to organise such a number of men from the police on such a large scale that is to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked a similar question by a member of the Trial Chamber, Judge Olivera Andjelkovic in Belgrade, on page English 59 and in Serbian it's page 46, and then on page 47. And on page 47, you say, answering to the question, "Local, could it be local or a wider level?" And you say: "What do you mean? It was the same everywhere. In Brcko there was a man with a pony-tail and in sneakers and he would say I am the commander of the police ..." And so on and so forth. Please have a look at paragraph 1 on page 47, "Where it was very dangerous," it says, "to kill a man. Immediately he would kill you. He came there and he was killing ...," and so on and so forth, "he was not -- he did not report to anyone if you looked at him he would kill you." So you were aware then that the local forces cannot deal with you or put up any resistance unless they got some reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, police is quite a strong force. If it is well organised, as in Brcko, there were almost 90 active duty policemen plus the reserve composition of the police. The groups that arrived were always numbering 15, 16, 20 men. As soon as they arrived, the paramilitaries would enter the SUP, and it's interesting that they would enter the SUP, they would introduce themselves, and say we are such-and-such forces, we are the Eagles, we are Arkan's men, we are the Red Berets, and they would take over the positions and everyone in the SUP would keep silent from the superiors to active-duty policemen, and wait to see what these men would do. This is something I could never understand. When I came to a SUP, particularly when she asked me about Brcko, it's correct, I came in front of the Brcko SUP building and a young man who was wearing some sort of camouflage uniform and a hat on his head, he was wearing white sneakers and he had gloves without the tops of the fingers with a Heckler in his hands, and he asked me, "Who are these men?" And I said, "Well, I'm the chief inspector, Davidovic." And I asked him, "Who are you?" And he said, "I'm the station commander." And again he asked me, "Who are you? What do you want?" I had to tell him, "I am the state." What else can you say to such a person at such a moment? I am the state. I am the official state organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He would say that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that. And immediately I would arrest him on the spot. People I had with me were quite well trained to one single sign from me. They could take care of such a man. This -- so this is what I did. So when I arrested three, four, or five men that I found in the SUP, at that moment the situation would change. A new situation would arise. Those who were not really official members of the organ would try to flee, try to hide, and I would reconstitute the active duty policemen, who would begin to work. We would have to go to the municipality, we had to take over the municipal building and we would reinstate the legal organs which had to do their work. We were doing this in Brcko, in Bijeljina and in Zvornik. In Zvornik, it was somewhat more difficult, but we did the same there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me remind you, do you remember and do you agree that Andan in his analysis about Brcko said that they are grateful to the army, that it allowed 120 or 150 policemen to return from the front line? The fact that regular police had to go out onto defence lines, was it something that also had a negative impact on the implementation of law and order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not want to comment on what Dragan Andan said and which you presented to me. I passed over it in silence for a simple reason. You are angry when I'm not answering by saying yes or no but provide explanations, but once again I'm in a situation where I have to say something. In Brcko, members of the reserve force were those who committed crimes. Jelisic wore a police member's uniform. He was a policeman, a reserve policeman. What happened? They came from Bijeljina to liberate them, and they sent active duty policemen to the front line and people from the outside came in such as Jelisic, Sasa, Pejo. They're all the same types, one criminal next to another, and they took over the power. So imagine Jelisic who gives him -- himself the right to mistreat people. If people were standing in a line to get a passport he would take someone out of the line, take out a gun and kill him. He's a member of the police, reserve police and it was passed over in silence by police officials and active duty policemen, by the military, by the leadership. No one said a word. The members of the Crisis Staff thought that the liberators had come, those who were the liberators believed that they came to do whatever they liked and they did do that. So the whole problem was that police mixed with such criminals. They were commanded by Pejo, by one Sasa or some Legija and so on, and without right to decide anything or do anything about that. This man would kill someone in the street and he would remain a member of the forces legally without anyone even asking him, How come you did that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until they sent Andan to make an assessment, and on the basis of assessment, they invited you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once an assessment was made and when the leadership of the Crisis Staff realised what was happening then they asked me and begged me. I was supposed to go to Zvornik first and they said, first go to Brcko, please. We have finished this. It's a question of one day or the next when we would all be killed. And if you allow me I will tell you another detail which I deem to be interesting. While we were discussing with the Crisis Staff in Brcko, on the premises of the MUP, and deputy Beli was also there he was the president of the executive council of Markovic, I think was his name and the garrison commander was there, the chief of the SUP, and even the priest from Brcko was present. Seven or eight people were there at the Crisis Staff. And while we were talking I noticed that some vehicles, jeeps without roofs were circling around the MUP building. People wearing hats on their heads, dangerous guys as one might call them. The dogs of war, the criminals who managed to get weapons. They were circling around the MUP and one of the people from my escort entered and said, "Commander, it seems that we are encircled." The leadership was frightened. It was a very complex situation. We went outside and I told them, Don't be afraid. I went outside of the building a minute or two later. Four, five vehicles arrived and some young men came out, but the men I had with me were highly trained. They were Specials. I need to explain that the Special is someone who was trained at the police and had been trained for years to carry out special tasks. They don't do patrols. They just do exercises. They do Judo, shooting exercises, and so on. They can do anything that is requested. I had 15 such mean with me, and quite understandably, I went outside. When they approached me one of them asked me, "Who is the boss here?" They would point me. I was standing next to a vehicle. They asked me who I was and what I wanted to Brcko. I was armed as well. After a few seconds, I would just give a sign to the police and in two minutes they would have them all down on the ground. We would have a van, and we would put 10 or 12 people inside, and we would quickly drive to Bijeljina to get out of the encirclement. After 10 or 15 minutes, they would call me by a radio from Brcko, "Mico Davidovic, do you hear us?" I wouldn't answer and then Lieutenant-Colonel Milicevic - I cannot remember his name - called me and said, "Please, Davidovic, can you answer." I could see it was serious. I would answer and then I would get one of those who had remained in Brcko and he would say, "Unless you release those you have arrested, we will kill a man every five minutes, a deputy, a commander of the staff, and so on." So how can I react otherwise than say feel free to kill them? "You have no reason not to kill them but remember I will arrest you all. I have you now. You cannot leave Brcko. I will have you." And then they would say, "Well, we're not going to leave Brcko, only with our legs forward, that is to say, dead." So that was the end of that part. We would arrest them in the morning, in the early hours at 2.30 a.m. we would enter Brcko just as we did in Zvornik then we would release people from the hangar. We would go and find the Red Berets who were quartered there. They were criminals, they had truck trailers full of goods, they were about to depart, and then once we had done all that, we would organise a meeting with the Crisis Staff. After that, we would have a meeting with the police. Usually the deputy minister or the minister himself, Mico, would arrive. We briefed him about what we did and ten days later, or three or four days, we would maintain the situation until the newly appointed commander and everyone else began to work properly and the police station began to function as it should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this vivid description. Just another question on page 86 in Serbian and 108 in English about a conversation or, rather, cross-examination. Branko Grujic asked you whether you knew that he personally went to see Radovan Karadzic together with the chief of the SUP to tell them that he couldn't live because of these people in Zvornik any more. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can see what the time is. Unless the Trial Chamber allows me some time tomorrow, I would like to thank you, Mr. Davidovic, and to express my regret that I did not see you before the trial just in order to specify some terminological imprecisions because I think a great deal of the problems arise from precise formulations which are very important for me as the Defence, whether it is the Crisis Staff or the staff of Territorial Defence or the War Presidency and so on, and we have to clarify what is rumour, and what is libel or slander, and what is something that is really certain information. Thank you for doing what you did when you helped in maintaining law and order there.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to thank you. I'm sorry that in my capacity as a witness I said what I have, but I really tried to say only the truth, which is not pleasant at all. The truth is such as it is. From the very beginning, I said everything as it was. I never imagined anything. I just said what the situation was like, what I did, who I contacted with, who I talked to. There is no need for me to distort anything, to say anything that I don't know directly. I am a serious man. I have a family. I wouldn't allow myself to do that, but, Mr. Karadzic, you tried to communicate with me or rather your Defence team and, unfortunately, you tried to do that through Cican Simic, the one who is mentioned in all these orders, and no one from the Prosecutor's office or the Tribunal knew that before. I didn't even know that I would be a witness here, nor did anyone tell me that I would come to testify as a Prosecution witness in your trial. And I must admit that I reflected earlier and I even told that to the Prosecution when I testified the second time with Mr. Stanisic, I said, please, don't invite me again. I am not a paid witness. I have had some unpleasant situations because of that. Please do not invite me, do not summon me. If I do not have to be a witness, try to find a resolution so that I don't have to be a witness in the Karadzic trial. However, I was requested to have a meeting without the Prosecutor's office or ICTY knowing about that, and I refused any such contact because I thought that was sidestepping legal organs and institutions. I think it was even blackmail because of some proceedings that were in progress, and I simply said I'm not going to talk with anyone from your side. That was the main reason. Apart from that, when I was a Prosecution witness in the Stanisic case, I talked to his Defence and Mr. Stanisic, as far as I know, as far as I learned through his Defence team, did not complain about my testimony. He said what he said is true, and I cannot refute what is true. This is the reason why I was slightly surprised about the way you tried to communicate with me, sometimes angrily insulting me and questioning my integrity and my family. But you have the right to defend yourself. I understood you. It's not pleasant for you, it's not pleasant for us, but this is a job that we all have to do; it's simply like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Davidovic, I have to say something to you. We talked to 80 per cent of the witnesses here and also this last question I have for you, please. Do you have any proof of my brother Luka or my son having a single commercial enterprise with Republika Srpska or knowing Vojkan. Let us try to see specifically what is a rumour and what is not. I am saying to you that my family was not involved in any kind of business because I had prohibited that and none of them know Vojkan.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I know this from Vojkan and from persons close to him that through him he was establishing contact with you. I don't know how true that is. He also mentioned Momo's brother there as well. He didn't say I went directly to President Karadzic. He said through Luka, I took care of all of that, and so and so forth. You know full well who Vojkan Djurkovic is. I don't know whether this Court had the opportunity of seeing him. He's a very dangerous type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely negative, an absolutely negative person. He is what he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Davidovic. We tried to conclude your evidence today, but evidently Madam Uertz-Retzlaff wants to have some further re-examination tomorrow morning. So we rise today and we'll begin tomorrow morning at 9.00. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Davidovic is coming back tomorrow, can the Defence have a bit more time just to deal with one particular topic, just to see what rumours are and what facts are, to spell that out precisely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will have a quarter of an hour tomorrow morning, but please bear in mind the Chamber is not interested in rumours. Tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 1st day of July, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.04 p.m.,
